On the Orders of the Day being called:

Mr. Speaker, I want to call your attention to a question of privilege. I notice in this morning's Citizen the announcement that I took luncheon yesterday with the hon. Minister of Militia and Defence (Mr. Hughes). That statement is absolutely contrary to the fact. I do not wish it for a moment to be understood that I object to lunching with the Minister of Militia in his private capacity. I have always found him in private life a man of very great personal charm, and in case there should be any doubt on the point, I would like to have it understood that I am rather open for an opportunity. But the gathering of yesterday appears to have been purely one of military celebrities. I am not eligible to meet such gentlemen, and I want it to be understood by this House and the country that I was not there, lest my well known reputation as a man of peace should be compromised.
Right Hon. R. L. BORDEN (Prime Minister) moved the third reading of Bill No.
21, to authorize measures for increasing the effective Naval. Forces of the Empire.

Mr. Speaker, I desire to say a tew final words in connection with this Bill, which has occupied the time of this House so long and which has attracted a considerable degree of attention throughout the country. We have spent a lot of time over the discussion of this Bill, both in its initial stages and in committee, but I really think, Sir, that notwithstanding the fact that a good deal of time has been occupied, that there have been some compensating advantages. If the discussion has done nothing else, it has established the fact that in this House are men who, for oratory, for precise argument, for tactical knowledge and for physical endurance, are the equals of the members of any deliberative assembly in the world. I do not intend to occupy the time of the House at any length, and I think that I will keep quite within a reasonable distance of closure limitations. It has been said, and is being said, that Parliament should be unanimous on this question of aid to the British naval service. I wish to state, Sir, and I believe that in this I voice the feelings and opinions of every hon. gentleman on this side of the House, that we desire to have this Parliament united on this great question and that we have shown our desire to have both Parliament and the people of the country united upon it. If we are not united on this question, the one man who is responsible is the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Borden) himself. He is the father of this Bill, he is the gentleman who introduced it. It has been stated in this House, time after time, and I wish to repeat it, that everything that can be done under the Naval Aid Act, which we are now asked to read a third time, can be done under the Naval Service Act, which the right hon. Prime Minister assisted in placing on the statute-book, and which he at that time approved of. Hon. gentlemen have been challenged to deny or controvert that statement if possible. There has never been a word uttered in contradiction of it.
It cannot be successfully contradicted that everything that can be done under this Act can be done under the Naval Service Act with the approval of Parliament. Who says that Parliament should not approve ? Shall the Governor in Council control this subject or shall Parliament control it ? When we have stated that, we have stated practically the issue between the parties in this contest. That being so, why should the right hon. gentleman have introduced this Bill, which he knew would be a contentious Bill and which he knew the Liberals of this House and the country could not accept if they Mr. BORDEN
were to be consistent with the record of the past ? He knew that the very same principle was embodied in the Highways Bill, introduced last year by the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Cochrane). He knew that the Liberals opposed that Highways Bill because it took out of the control of Parliament the expenditure of a million dollars of public money and placed that control in the hands of a minister of the Crown absolutely and only to do as he saw fit, either in any one year, or in succeeding years, and at such times as he desired to spend the money. He knew that this was a contentious Bill, but, notwithstanding that, he saw fit to oast into the arena of politics a Bill which he knew the Liberals could not accept. The	right hon.
gentleman was equally responsible with us for the passing of	the^ Naval
Service Act. There was no dissension if I remember rightly, he moved that the ships, when built, should be placed at the service of the British Admiralty whenever necessary, and that Parliament should have no voice in the matter. That was disputed for a time, but hon. gentlemen opposite conceded that proposition to the then Government, and the Bill passed practically without a dissenting voice on the part of hon. gentlemen opposite except that the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) moved that it should first receive the approval of the people of Canada. The proposition of the right hon. gentleman did not attack in any way the principle of the Bill; therefore I say that he is equally responsible with us for the passing of the Naval Service Act. Why then should he insist on forcing through Parliament a Bill which he can do no more than he can do under the Naval Service Act, especially in view of the fact that it creates dissension in this country'! If the Government had taken proceedings under the Naval Service Act, this aid to the British Admiralty for maintaining the supremacy of the British Empire upon the sea would have been given unanimously. My right hon. friend, however, launched into the arena of politics this Bill which he knew we were bound to oppose. The only reason that can be given for his action, that has been stated and that has not been contradicted, is that the righ t hon. gentleman is bound and gagged by his Nationalist colleagues from the province of Quebec. Let him come back to the position which he occupied in 1910. Let him cast his Nationalist colleagues overboard. Similar action was taken in years gone by when old Jonah was cast overboard to calm the raging tempest. Let him do the same here and calm the raging tempest of to-day; then he can build his ships and launch them in still waters.

Does the hon. member mean to say that the Nationalists have not

voted with the Opposition against the Naval Bill?
No.

The hon. gentleman is
mistaken. Some of them have voted against the Government in order to save their political hides when they go back to their constituents, because they are pledged to vote against any sort of naval aid to Great Britain.
There is no reason why both parties should not get together on this question. I propose to give my right hon. friend and hon. gentlemen opposite another chance to join with us, so that whatever is done will be done unanimously. Before I sit down, I intend to move in amendment a motion similar to the one I moved in Committee of the Whole, namely:
That upon appropriations in that behalf being from time to time made by Parliament, there may be paid and applied from and out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund of Canada a sum not exceeding $35,000,000 for the purpose of speedily increasing the effective naval forces of the Empire.
My right hon. friend expressed himself a few days ago as though that amendment would be of no effect. As reported on page 9669 of ' Hansard,' he stated that I was willing to make an appropriation under the Naval Service Act at once, and if that appropriation were made all these dreadful powers would be vested in the Governor in Council immediately. I deny that absolutely. If this amendment is ad pted, the money will be voted eventually, but it will be voted from year to year. He further said:
I would like to point out to the hon. gentleman that we are asking for an appropriation and we are also consulting Parliament as to the purpose for which that appropriation shall be applied. Therefore, Parliament is being consulted as effectually now and as freely as it could be under the provisions of the Naval Service Act of 1910.
I deny that absolutely and in toto. What do we find? Let us take a very apt illustration in connection with the construction of the Welland canal, the cost of which is estimated to be an amount similar to the cost of construction of these three dreadnoughts. The length of time required for the construction of that canal will be practically the same as for the construction of these dreadnoughts. My right hon. friend might just as well say that the Government could ask Parliament to appropriate $40,000,000 for the construction of a new Welland ship canal, the expenditure of which would extend over four years, as that they could ask Parliament to vote $35,000,000 for the construction of these three dreadnoughts, the expenditure of which will extend over at least three
years, and to place that money in the hands of a minister of the Crown to expend during that period. The cases are absolutely parallel. If Parliament has the right to vote an appropriation of millions of dollars, the expenditure of which shall extend over three or four years, it has just as much right to vote an appropriation of a hundred million dollars, the expenditure of which shall extend over ten, fifteen or twenty years, that money to be in the hands of a minister of the Crown and under his control during those years without Parliament having a word to say in the matter. The right hon. gentleman would not introduce such a proposition, much less support it, in this House; but that is what he is endeavouring to do by this Bill. He says: Oh, but the Governor General in Council under the Naval Service Act has the right to purchase supplies. Certainly, and the Governor General in Council has the right under any Act of Parliament to expend the public money- for how long without the approval of Parliament? For three years? Not at ail. For one year, and one year only, and then the Government have to come to Parliament and give an account of their stewardship to the people whose servants they are. That is what we insist on and that is what is embodied in the Naval Service Act. That is the principle which my right hon. friend supported in 1910, but which he is violating at this moment in connection with the Naval Aid Bill.
Are you in favour of the principle of this Bill, that is, of the purchase of three of the largest dreadnoughts in the world?

I do not see that I can explain my attitude more clearly than I have done. If my right hon. friend will withdraw this Bill now and take action under the Naval Service Act, which he helped to place on the statute book, and ask for an appropriation-he says $10,000,000-towards the building of dreadnoughts in Great Britain, I for one will support that proposition and I believe the Liberals, in the province of Ontario at any rate, will support it. But no, we will not do that. Why? Because he is pledged to the Nationalists to repeal that Act.
Then, do I understand the hon. gentleman to say that he would be in favour of this Bill if the amount were voted yearly instead of in one sum?

As I have said, time and time again, I am not in favour of this Bill at all, because it involves principles subversive of every principle that Liberals have fought for since time immemoral. My hon. friend seems to think that there is nothing in the question of the expenditure of money

being controlled by the Governor in Council as against being controlled by Parliament. Sir, I stated before and I state again, that that question was one of the burning questions in Canada in 1834-5-6-7. It was one of the questions which created a rebellion in Upper Canada at that time. Let hon. gentlemen look at the report of the committee of grievances made in 1835, the chairman of which was William Lyon Mackenzie. That report says, speaking of the British constitution:
The annual assembly of Parliament was rendered necessary in the first place by the strict appropriation of the revenue according to the votes of supply. No such system of checks and balances to protect from executive usurpation of popular right can he found in Upper Canada.
And, Sir, throughout the whole history of that time that was one of the burning questions; and this right of Parliament to control expenditure was one of the principles established at that time-unfortunately with bloodshed and death, but firmly established-in the constitution of Canada. From that moment, never an attempt was made to override or interfere in any way with the operation of that principle until 1870, when the coalition government of John Sandfield Macdonald passed through the legislature at Toronto a Bill similar to the one which my right hon. friend is now asking us to pass, which appropriated $1,500,000 to be handed over to the Lieutenant Governor in Council to be used by them in aid of the construction of railroads without any supervision or control thereof by Parliament. Edward Blake, as has already been said, opposed that proposition and said it was subversive of the principle of the Canadian constitution. The parties, in 1871, went to the people of the province of Ontario on that issue and that issue alone, and on that issue, and that issue alone, the Government of John Sandfield Macdonald was defeated, showing that the people of Ontario saw the absolute necessity of maintaining the popular rights which they had achieved in 1837. No other similar attempt was made until, when? Last year this Government introduced their Highways Bill embodying exactly the same principle. The sixth clause of that Bill provided that $1,000,000 could be spent by the minister of 'the Crown as he saw fit. That was the principle involved, and that was the principle we in this House of Commons combatted. And that was the principle on which the Senate voted when they amended the Bill by "striking out that clause. That same principle is involved in the Bill now before this House. I have been charged with saying that the Senate would throw out this Bill. I did say so. I do not know what the Senate will do, speaking from knowledge; I know no more about what the Sen-Mr. GERMAN.
ate will do in regard to this Bill than does any other hon. member of this House. But I do know this, that the principles which dominate in the Senate to-day are the principles of the Liberal party, the principles held on this side of the House. If these principles are as well lounded in the Senate as they are on this side of this House then that Bill cannot live long after it reaches the Senate.
My right hon. friend the Prime Minister is going to Toronto, and will, without doubt, on next Monday night, address an assembly large in numbers'-
Hear, hear.

-as did my right hon. leader a week ago-large in numbers and strong in enthusiasm. I would like the right hon. gentleman to take the message to the people of Toronto, and I would like this message to go to the uttermost parts of this great Dominion:	That we on this
side of the House desire to join gentlemen on the opposite side of the House in putting through Parliament a measure of aid to the British naval service which will be unanimous and will be approved by the people, aid which when granted will be of real assistance to Great Britain by reason of the fact that the united sentiment of Canada is behind it. I want him to take this message, that if he will go back to where he stood in 1909 and 1910, we can be unanimous. If he will adopt the amendment that I am moving now and the other amendments which will be moved, and which are similar to those that we have already moved, we then can get together on this question. If he will but refrain from going back on every record of the past, every utterance that he made in this House in 1909 and 1910; if he will stand by the Bill which he helped to place on the statute-book in 1910, we shall be a united people and the ships can be built and sent forth to aid the British service in any portion of the seas. That is the proper thing for the Government to do; that is what we have been struggling for and are struggling for now. And, though we shall have no further opportunity-and want no further opportunity so far as that is concerned-of discussing this matter in this House, we should like to see unanimity; we should like to see the proposition suggested by my hon. friend from South York (Mr. Maclean) carried out when he urged that in this matter all parties in Canada should
-run
Like the horses of the sun,
All abreast.
For these reasons, I am pleased to move the amendment which I now have the honour to place in your hands:

That this Bill be not now read a third time, but that it be referred back to the Committee of the Whole House with instructions to strike out Clause 2 thereof, and substitute the following:
Upon appropriations in that behalf being from time to time made by Parliament, there may be paid and applied from and out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund of Canada a sum not exceeding $35,000,000 for the purpose of speedily increasing the effective naval forces of the Empire.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. L. BORDEN (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend who has just taken his seat (Mr. German) so far as I am able to appreciate his remarks, has said nothing on the present occasion that he has not already said on two or three previous occasions; and, as I then endeavoured to make what answers seemed to be appropriate, he will pardon me if I do not follow him at any very great length now. He has urged upon us that nothing could be done under this Bill which could not be done under the Naval Service Act of 1910 with an appropriation. I repeat that if that be the case it i3 utterly inconceivable to me why the hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House should have presented the opposition that they have presented to this Bill. It does no more, says the hon. gentleman, than can be done under the Naval Service Act of 1910; and yet they oppose it to the last gasp and declare that it is absolutely subversive of every principle of Liberalism. My hon. friend is not very logical, and, more than that, he is not very accurate; because, in referring to our attitude on the Naval Service Bill of 1910, he has stated that the Conservative party in this House, including myself, supported that Bill. I wish to inform the hon. gentleman -and he can verify my statement by reference to the records-that that Bill went to a vote upon the third reading, and that it was carried by a vote of 111 to 70, a majority of 41. He asks me why I do not go back to the policy of 1910. Does he remember the policy that we advocated in 1910? I shall read to him one clause of it. moved by myself on the second reading. It was as follows:
That the immediate duty of Canada and the impending necessities of the Empire can best he discharged and met by placing without delay at the disposal of the Imperial authorities, as a free and loyal contribution from the people of Canada, such an amount as may be sufficient to purchase or construct two battleships or armoured cruisers of the latest dreadnought type, giving to the Admiralty full discretion to expend the said sum at such time and for such purposes of naval defence as in their judgment may best serve to increase the united strength of the Empire and thus assure its peace and security.
And yet the bon. gentleman suggests that we are departing from the policy which
we advocated on that occasion. I take exception to his remarks and join absolute issue with him. My hon. Mend has repeated that there is some understanding or agreement between the Liberal-Conservative party and certain gentlemen in Quebec whom he describes as Nationalists. He has repeated that, notwithstanding my assurance to him on two previous occasions during the present session that there was no pledge an.l no promise that had not been made public. Since he has introduced the subject, I would tell him that I myself, sitting in this House, heard the chief of the Nationalists, state that he was putting forward no principle and that he propounded no policy that he had not learned from my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier); and I would remind him further-
I think he has backslid.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: -that while he stated his principles and his policy, he declared in the hearing of the House at that time-and my right hon. friend did not 'contradict him-
I did not contradict him, but he has fallen from grace since.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
My right hon. friend did not contradict the statement made by him on that occasion. That gentleman, being then a member of the House, stated that his principles and policies respecting the defence of the Empire were what he had learned from the right hon. leader of the Opposition. I remind the hon. member for Welland of this, because he is very fond, apparently for some purpose which he may consider advantageous to his political interest, of making an assertion which has already been contradicted over and over again. I would point out to him that when in 1908 an attack was made in this House upon some gentlemen who were described as Nationalists, in respect of a cartoon, a copy of which I hold in my hand, published in one of fheir newspapers, certain facts were disclosed which do not at all support the suggestion of my hon. friend from Welland, but rather support the suggestion that he himself is in alliance with the Nationalists, if he is a good member of the party opposite. What was the cartoon? It represented Jean Baptiste with both hands on the Union Jack and an Imperialist uttering to him the following admonition:
' Hold on to the flag, Baptiste, as Dundon-ald said, and I will hold your coat for you.' The Imperialist is represented as pilfering the pockets of the simple-minded and credulous Jean Baptiste. When we came to investigate the facts, we found that that cartoon had not originally appeared in a Nationalist newspaper at all, but had appeared in Le Canada, the acknowledged

organ of the Liberal party in Quebec, in the election campaign of 1904, after a certain incident in connection with the dismissal or retirement of Lord Dundonald. The very material which was put forward as an example of Nationalist perfidy and disloyalty was material till at had been taken from the columns of the Liberal organ in the province of Quebec. Under these circumstances, although I do not desire to go into that question at any length, I think it ill becomes the hon. member for Welland discuss the subject of alleged alliances.
He has seen fit to reiterate the suggestion that I am responsible for any dissension in this House with regard to this measure. I take exception to it in the strongest possible terms. I submitted these proposals to this House in a non-controversial speech, and I produced a memorandum from the Admiralty which, as I understood, imposed upon Canada the duty of taking some step of an immediate and effective character to aid in the naval defence of the Empire. In thus placing my proposals before this Parliament I followed the advice oi the Admiralty as I understood it. I brought that' measure before this House in no controversial manner, by no controversial speech; and I had no reason to expect that it would meet the opposition which unfortunately has been manifested in this House. I am desirous, as much as any man in the House can be, that any aid of this character should go forth to the Mother Country, not only by the unanimous voice of the people of Canada, but, so far as may be possible, by the unanimous voice of this House. But, under the circumstances to which I have alluded, I do not think the hon. gentleman is justified in any sense or from any standpoint in imputing to me the lack of union between the two parties which has made itself manifest in respect of this measure. I have already shown that what we propose can be harmonized with what has already been put forward by hon. gentlemen opposite, both in 1910 and during the present session, before these ships can be put in commission, if it should be the will of the Canadian people that fleet units should be established and that a naval organization on a large scale should be undertaken by the people of Canada in the immediate future. There can be no possible difficulty about that, even if this measure should be passed. Under these circumstances, I venture to express once more my very great surprise that hon. gentlemen opposite, especially my hon. friend from Welland, should have manifested the insistent opposition to this measure which has made itself apparent ever since we placed it before the House.
Mr. BOUDEN.

Before you put the motion, Mr. Speaker, I wish to move an amendment on this question of naval defence which will assert once more the rights of Canada, our common country.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. There are too
many hon. members talking. That is distinctly a violation of the rules, which say .that when an hon. member is on his feet there must be no noise.

I rise to say a word on behalf of Canada on this momentous question. Sir, we are all devoted to the British Empire, but we are all devoted also to Canada, our native land. It seems to me that if the Canadians of 1867, the fathers of Confederation-Sir John A. Macdonald, Sir George Cartier, George Brown, and Alexander Mackenzie-at that remote period of our national existence, foresaw that Canada could organize her defence not only on land, but on sea, we, living in the year of our Lord, 1913, should not go backwards, but should follow in their footsteps. In 1868, a Conservative administration went to defeat because it had the courage to establish wdiat is to-day known as the Canadian Militia. Our volunteer force was finally established; the Militia Act is on our statute book, and our gallant soldiers are serving His Majesty the King under the British flag. It is a Canadian militia, commanded by Canadian officers, and by Canadian generals, and yet no one would dare suggest that because of that, the volunteer force is a separatist organization. As Canada developed and progressed, the time came when it was thought proper to have a naval force on sea for the protection of our trade, for the defence of our coasts on the Atlantic and Pacific, and at the same time as our due share of contribution to the naval defence of the Empire in cases of real emergency. Canada started to organize her navy as she had organized

If the hon gentleman will permit me, I would quote what the right hon. the Prime Minister (Mt. Borden) stated on the 7th April, as reported at page 7411 of 'Hansard.' He said:
I desire, speaking upon my responsibility as a member of this Government, to take the strongest possible exception to the statements which the right hon. gentleman has made. I say, in the first place, that it is not a policy of contribution at all, and I say, in the second place, that it is not a permanent policy. That was stated on the 5th day of December last, I have stated it on more than one occasion since, and I state it again to-day in the strongest form of expression that parliamentary usage will permit.

My hon. friend might
take ' Hansard ' of 1909 and 1910, and find exactly the contrary of what his leader has said in the sentence he has just quoted.
Sir, this is a permanent policy of contribution; yes, it is the establishment of tribute in this free country of Canada. This policy is un-Canadian; it is un-British. It spells distrust, not trust. It divides the people of this country. It pleases the jingoes alone; it does not satisfy Canadian pride and Canadian manhood, and manly Britishers the world over will say that it is not in the best interests of the Empire. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I move the following amendment:
That the said Bill be not now read a third time, but that it be referred back to the Committee of the Whole for the purpose of amending the same by providing that all works under this Act shall be executed under the provisions of the Naval Service Act.

Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend from Rouville (Mr. Lemieux), and indeed nearly every hon. gentleman opposite, have been repeating time and again-I might almost call it tiresome reiteration-that this is part of the permanent naval policy of the present Government. I can quite appreciate why it is absolutely necessary for hon. gentlemen opposite to make that contention, because they know that, unless they can prove it to be founded upon fact, they are absolutely inconsistent with regard to their prior action in regard to naval service in Canada. In 1910, when they brought in their naval policy, which they admitted was their permanent naval policy, they refused to go to the country on it though it was admittedly their permanent policy. They know that we submitted a counter pro-

position for the purpose of giving temporary relief to then existing conditions in the Empire by contributing a sum of money sufficient to build two dreadnoughts. ' They know that, unless they can make the people believe that this is our permanent policy, they 'have no ground whatever for asking Parliament to submit this measure to the people. They know that the Prime Minister has said that he intends to submit his permanent naval policy to the people. They know that, before he was called to power, he said that he would go to England; that he would take the evidence of the British Admiralty, the best possible evidence that could be obtained, in order to find out the true situation. He went there and did so. It is perfectly well known to the British Admiralty that this is not the permanent policy of Canada. It was well known in the House of Commons, when the Prime Minister was in England that this was not the permanent policy. I just wish to read from the speech which Mr. Winston Churchill made in the British House of Commons at that time, in order to prove my contention. I am quoting from Mr. Churchill's speech in the House of Commons on July 22, last, when he said:
There is, however, a strong distinction between measures which deal with the requirements of the immediate future and the elaboration of a permanent naval policy. The latter will require longer consideration and much fuller discussion than have been possible during the short time our visitors have been among us. Mr. Borden and his colleagues authorize me to say they share this view, and that any special action which the immediate future may require of them will not be delayed pending the settlement of a final and permanent naval arrangement.
That shows conclusively that the Prime Minister told them that this was no part of his permanent naval policy, but that the latter would require a great deal of discussion and consideration in this country. He told them that this is simply a measure of temporary relief, and that the permanent policy would be submitted to the people. In view of the declarations of the right hon. the Prime Minister, when on the 5th day of December last he said that this was no part of the permanent policy of the Government, and that his permanent policy would be submitted to the people, and when, on the 7th of April, he said: I have again and again reiterated in this House that this is no part of the permanent naval policy of the country; it is simply an emergency provision, is it fair for hon. members opposite to contend that this measure is part of the permanent policy of the Government? Is it fair for them to issue campaign literature, a copy of which I have before me now, which on the face of it says that the policy of this Government is to contribute $35,000,000 as part of the permanent naval policy of this Mr. MIDDLEBRO.
country? They are disseminating that information throughout the country, for the purpose of endeavouring to make the people believe that to be true which is not true.

Is my hon.
friend's conception of Imperial Federation, which has been mentioned in this House and also by Mr. Churchill, wrapped up in the idea of one contribution?

I simply say to my hon. friend that this House has the absolute right to make whatever gift it chooses to make. It may make a gift to a foreign nation for the purpose of affording relief in the case of an earthquake disaster or on account of floods, and it has done so. In doing so, Parliament is exercising its undoubted democratic parliamentary right, and that is exactly what we are doing here to-day. We, on this side of the House, state that we will grant to the British Admiralty $35,000,000 for the purpose of building three dreadnoughts in order to assist Great Britain in maintaining her supremacy upon the sea.
I have had letters from Liberals in my riding stating that, if I can show them that the Prime Minister has stated openly and publicly that this is not part of the permanent naval policy of this country, they will vote for the policy brought in by him. When the Prime Minister says that this is not part of his permanent policy, are we not to believe him? Do hon. gentlemen opposite want this to be part of our permanent policy? If they do not, why do they preach that it is? The only answer is, they know they are absolutely inconsistent in asking Parliament to submit this measure to the people, unless they can deceive the people into believing that it is part of the permanent policy of the Government, when they know that it is not.	*

policy of the right hon. Prime Minister, I suppose it is the Montreal Star. We had the policy announced by the correspondent, Windermere, in the Montreal Star read in this House by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, and given us as authority on which we ought to vote. The Montreal Star said:
We are fighting in this country for ' one navy ' This is not because there are no peo-f pie in Canada who would like to have the feeding, and handling, and building, and incidental ' grafting ' that would go with a Canadian navy. But we realize that the navy is ail instrument which can best be managed by a central authority; and that, if the Em-, pire is not valuable as a means of controlling a great British navy, it is hard to see why it is valuable at all. For what then are we to use the Empire? Why should we stay m it? Obviously, if it is to he anything but an empty shell, it ought to look after the navy.
There you have the statement of the leading organ cf the Conservative party in regard to what we ought to do. I submit that the reiterated statements of the right hon. Prime Minister, the statements of nis press and of the men who sit behind him go to prove that they are in favour of a policy of contribution.

At one o'clook I had
pointed out that several prominent men supporting my right hon. friend had declared themselves in favour of an Imperial navy to be supported by a -contribution system. I wish now to state that my right hon. friend himself on the 27th of February this year used language in this House which cannot be understood in any other way, I submit, excepting in the way that we contend he has been drifting, and that is in favour of a system of contribution. Speaking on that date, as reported at page 387 of 'Hansard,' he used the following language:
Now, I come to one or two other points and I shall endeavour to be as brief as possible in dealing with them. What will be the purpose of the navy which my hon. friends propose to create when it is created? They propose to have one fleet unit on the Atlantic and one fleet unit on the Pacific. For what purposes will they be placed there and to what extent will they be effective? I say that the defence of Canada will be by the united naval forces of the whole Empire and I further maintain that it would be impossible for a single fleet unit on the Atlantic, or a single fleet unit on the Pacific, to defend the shores or coast line of Canada against such an attack as might be expected if an attack were to take place. On the other hand, if you have the British navy, the most powerful navy in the world, if you co-operate with it, if you assist in maintaining and building it up, I venture to say that you have
Mr. SINCLAIR.
arrived, for the present at least, at the best solution of this problem that could possibly be devised and in support of this I take the clear statement of the Admiralty that the best way in which Canada can aid the Empire at the present time is by the provision of a certain number of the strongest and most powerful battleships that money can procure or science can devise.
What does that declaration mean ? It means that a Canadian navy could not be effective, and are we to assume that my right hon. friend would support a navy that he believes would not be effective ? He makes the positive statement that in his opinion a navy such as can be built up in Canada would not be useful in protecting the coasts of Canada. Can we expect my right hon. friend to embark on the construction of a navy of this kind which in his opinion would not be useful for the purpose for which it was built ? He further says that if we assist in maintaining the British navy that would be the best solution of the difficulty. I submit that that language is very plain. I do not know what my right hon. friend could say that would be any plainer as to his attitude in regard to this question, as distinguishing between a Canadian navy and a system of contribution to the Mother Country. He has not said in so many words that he is in favour of a system of contribution, but that is the only fair and honest inference that we can take from his language.

speechtext: I would suggest to the hon. member that he is wandering outside the amendment which is before the House. It is simply that all work under this Act should be executed under the provisions of the Naval Service Act.

I submit that I am
keeping closely to that very question. I am dealing with the question as to whether we should have a Canadian naval service or a system of contribution to the Mother Country. This matter is very easily settled. If my right hon. friend intends to embark on the construction of a Canadian navy in the future why does he not say so? Why does he not come out frankly and take us into his confidence? We do not expect him to give us the details of his policy, to say how many ships he is going to build, we do not expect him to say whether he will build the ships in Canada or elsewhere. We are not anxious to confine him to any details in regard to his policy but surely he is able to give us this information tliat he favours establishing at some time or other a Canadian navy. He has not ventured to make that statement during the whole course of this discussion. Why has he not said so? I submit that if he ventured to stand up in his place and make that statement this

afternoon a number of things would happen. The Postmaster General (Mr. Pelletier) would resign. The Minister of Inland Revenue (Mr. Nantel) would resign.
Never.
The hon. the Secretary of State (Mr. Coderre) would Tesign.
Never.

The Deputy Speaker
(Mr. Blondin) would resign.
Oh, no.

These things would
have to happen, because these men are pledged to this course and they are all honourable men. You see that there is a good reason why my right hon. friend does not come out and be frank with the House as to whether he is in favour of a Canadian navy or a system of contribution to the Mother Country.
There has been considerable speculation as to what course the Senate would take on this question. For my part, I cannot see how the Senate can take any but the one course. Senators supporting the present Administration and senators opposed to the present Administration have already voted in favour of a Canadian navy. Three years ago, with the unanimous consent of that Chamber, they passed a Bill in favour of a Canadian naval system, they have always declared themselves in favour of a Canadian navy and I submit that nothing has happened during the course of this debate to change the minds of the hon. gentlemen in the upper Chamber. The question then will be, will the Prime Minister keep the pledge that he gave to the people of Canada that if Parliament refused to pass this Bill he would immediately appeal to the people. Will he keep that pledge? There is, I submit only one way to settle this question, only one way to find out whether we should proceed with this policy, it is by an appeal to the Canadian people. I pointed out that when my right hon. friend went to the people in September 1911 he was very careful not to announce any naval policy. He therefore, has no mandate from the people of Canada, especially he has no mandate to take the step that he is proposing to take. He is therefore bound in honour to appeal to the country. That is one of the splendid things about the British system of public life. When a Prime Minister does not know, when he has a fair and reasonable doubt whether he has the country behind him, it is his duty to appeal to the people and find out what the will of the people is. In the United States, the President is appointed
for a certain period of years. The people throw the business of the country into his hands during that time, they have to submit to whatever he and his cabinet choose to do during that period. But that is not the British system, and that is one of the splendid things about the British system. We put out trust in the honour of men, we put our trust in the honour of ministers and especially of the Prime Minister and it is the bounden duty of the Prime Minister, if he has any reasonable doubt as to whether the people of Canada are in favour of the policy he is now proposing, he should appeal to the people and find out whether or not they will sustain him. We had his promise and I for one will trust him until he actually does break his word. It will not take us very long to find out, in a few days we will know what action the other Chamber will take and I hope that when that result is known the Prime Minister of Canada will be as good as his word and will dissolve Parliament, go to the country and find out what the will of the country is on this important question.

We have had some discussion to-day as to whether or not it would not have been better to have attempted to construct, under the Canadian Naval Service Act passed in 1910, the proposed vessels; and, so far as I have been able to follow the discussion, no reason has been given by my hon. friends opposite why they did not follow that course. It has been charged on this side of the House by many hon. members, that my right hon. friend the Prime Minister would not call for tenders or construct the ships under the Canadian Naval Service Act, Because his Nationalist allies would not permit him to do so. My right hon. friend has never tried to answer that question until to-day, and- to my recollection, about the only argument he advanced was a cartoon which' appeared in Le Canada some years ago, and which was afterwards reproduced in some other papers. That is a pretty lame excuse for the Prime Minister to offer for departing from a great constitutional principle, and for taking the course which the Government are taking on this important question. I wonder if there is another reason for the course which is being pursued by my right hon. friend. I know I am not allowed to impute motives to any hon. member of this House, but I am allowed to state facts, and if the public impute motives upon a knowledge of those facts, I am not responsible. I find in section 5 of the Canadian Naval Service Act the following:
There shall be a department of the Government of Canada which shall be called the Department of the Naval Service over which the Minister of Marine and Fisheries for the time being shall preside, and he shall be the Minister of the Naval Service.
Then I find in the Revised Statutes, vol. I, on page 39, the following:
Whenever any works are to be executed under the direction of any department of the Government, the minister having charge of such department shall invite tenders by public advertisement for the execution of such works, except in cases
(a)	of pressing emergency in which delay would be injurious to the public interest; or
(b)	in which from the nature of the work
Mr. SINCLAIR.

it can be more expeditiously and economically executed by the officers and servants of the department; or,
(c) Where the estimated cost of the work is less than five thousand dollars and it appears to the minister, in view of the nature of the work, that it is not advisable to invite tenders.
2. Whenever in case of any work tenders are required to be invited, the minister having charge of the department concerned shall submit all tenders received therefor to the Governor in Council and the contract for the work shall be awarded under the direction of the Governor in Council.
That is the law of Canada to-day, and, if my right hon. friend had decided to construct those vessels under the Naval Service Act, he would have been brought under the law as I have read it. I sometimes wonder if it is to evade the conditions of that law that my right hon. friend is pursuing the course he is taking to-day. Let us see where the suggestion lands us. Under the Naval Service Act those vessels would be constructed under a department of the Government, then they are brought within the terms of the section which I have read, that is the section which provides:	[DOT]
Whenever any works are to be executed under the direction of any department of the Government, the minister having charge of such department shall invite tenders.
Would there be anything to prevent the Government from calling for tenders for the construction of those three ships? The statute says positively that these public works shall be done after public tenders have been called for, except in cases
(a) of pressing emergency in which delay would be injurious to the public interest.
Well, Sir, my right hon. friend will not now say that there is a pressing emergency in this case. It is true that the hon. member for North Grey (Mr. Middlebro) had the assurance to go back to the old position of six months ago, and to say there was an emergency. He even went so far as to say that there is a crisis, but nobody but my hon. friend from North Grey would risk his reputation in making such statements. My right hon. friend the Prime Minister will not risk it. I venture to prophesy that he will not risk it in Toronto next Monday night. He has too much regard for the real condition of affairs, and for his reputation as a statesman, to make a statement like that. Everybody knows now that there is no question of an emergency. Time and again during the last three or four months, the British Government have reiterated that they are perfectly capable oh taking charge of any condition that may arise. They have all the ships 'they need, and all the men, and all the money, and they are ready to take care of
any situation that may arise. As has been pointed out a number of times, too, conditions have changed in Europe recently, and there is no emergency there. The second exception in the statute is a case:
In which from the nature of the work it can be more expeditiously and economically executed by the officers and servants of the department.
Well, my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries cannot build these vessels under his department, and therefore the case does not come under that exception. Then the third exception is:
Where the estimated cost of the work is less than five thousand dollars and it appears to the minister, in view of the nature of the work, that it is not advisable to invite tenders.
As this expenditure amounts to $35,000,000 or $40,000,000, it does not come under that exception. Therefore, if my right hon. friend had decided to build the vessels under the Canadian Naval Service Act, he would have been brought under the provisions of this law, and would have had to call for tenders. It is true that the department is not always under the necessity of accepting the lowest tender, but, if they do not accept the lowest tender, they have to coma to Parliament and give very good reasons why they have not. That is the law. I find that that course has been followed in every important undertaking in Canada in recent years. Even before the general law was passed, that principle was laid down definitely in connection with the greatest work which has been constructed by the Government during the last fifteen or twenty years, the National Transcontinental railway. In fact I might say that that is the only great work that has been constructed by the Government in Canada in the last fifteen years outside ot the ordinary run of public works for improvement of navigation, public wharves, and other works required to carry on the business of the country. When the National Transcontinental Railway Act was passed in 1903, nothing was left to the Government to do at their own sweet will. As I understand it, the section I have read regarding the necessity of calling for public tenders in connection with the construction of public works had not been passed, but in order that there should be no question about it, in order that the best results should be obtained for the least money, and that there should not be the least suspicion as to the integrity of the officials carrying out that great work, it was provided that the work must be done by tender. So religiously was that principle carried out in connection with the Transcontinental railway, that $50 contracts had to be let by tender, even although the com.

missioners thought they could do, better under an ordinary arrangement with some contractor. In every case they had to comply with the condition and call for tenders. You will find that condition in section 16, chapter 71 of the Statutes of 1903:
The commissioners shall let the work of constructing the eastern division by tender and contract after the plans and specifications therefor have been duly advertised, and they shall accept the lowest tender put in by a contractor who, in the judgment of the commissioners, is possessed of sufficient skill, experience and resources to carry on the work or such portion thereof as he has tendered for.
I have not looked up the history of that section, but my recollection is that it was moved by a prominent member of the then Opposition, now in the Government. My right hon. friend the Prime Minister will recollect the discussion, and - will remember that both parties insisted that that was the proper course to pursue, that the contracts must be let by tender. The result has been that, in the last seven or eight years from $100,000,000 to $120,000,000 worth of work has been done by public 'tender, and done so successfully and honestly that after investigating it for the last year and a half, after spending probably $50,000 in investigating it, and after sending not one, but half a dozen engineers half a dozen times all over the work, the Government have not been able to find one dollar's worth of work that has not been properly done. It is true that some of their inspecting engineers have said that the classification should not have been so high, but that is only a matter of judgment. They cannot find anything wrong, and now their chief investigator has given up the job in disgust and has been given a better one at $20,000 a year to look after the Intercolonial. This only shows you how important it is that the great public works should be carried on by public tender and contract. It shows that when we were carrying on a work costing $125,000,000 it was done so honestly that hon. members opposite could find no fault, and could pick no flaw in the management of it. Why should not this policy be adopted regarding the construction of these vessels? My right hon. friend said the other day, when I called this matter to his attention, that possibly the work could be best done in the Government dockyards. Besides the Government dockyards there are eight or nine different shipyards in Great Britain that build dreadnoughts. My right hon. friend proposes to get this work done in the Government dockyards, but if the conditions are such that he can get his vessels built in the shipyards of Cammell, Laird and Company, John Brown and Company, or Beardmore and Company or of any of the other large shipbuilders in Great Britain, on more reasonable terms Mr. CAEVELL.
than he can get them built in the Government shipyards, is that any reason why he should not have the advantage of all the information available, or is that any reason why he should not call for tenders for the building of these vessels?
He cannot make a contract for the construction of these vessels unless he has plans and specifications. He must be in a position to call for tenders before he is justified in signing any contract or spending a dollar. If he can find a private contracting firm in Great Britain who will build these vessels cheaper than he can have them built in the Government dockyards, surely he would be justified in having it done by them. How is my right hon. friend going to find out what these vessels will cost unless he calls for tenders? I am only appealing to my right hon. friend as an ordinary business man. I have tried to show him what has been the custom and what has been the law in Canada regarding the building of public works. In order to get around the law in Canada he is having a special statute passed in the form of a Bill, which is now before this Parliament, a Bill which takes away all the safeguards which have been thrown around the construction of public works for the last ten or fifteen years, a Bill which, if passed, would permit graft to run rampant and there would be no way of finding it out. I am not saying that the right hon. gentleman intends thai, there shall be graft, I am only pointing out that there could not be graft if he followed the ordinary law of the country, while under this Bill there could be millions of graft and the public have no opportunity of finding out what the true conditions are. I have no doubt that is the reason why hon. gentlemen opposite insist on bringing about this change. I have placed the law before my right hon. friend, I have shown him what the law is and what it would be if he took advantage of the ordinary machinery provided at the present time for the building of these vessels. But, without any reason, and without any explanation, he has created a new Bill which takes away all the protection, which removes every safeguard the ratepayers of Canada have at the present time and which gives him the absolute power to control the expenditure of public money up to the amount of $40,000,000. There is nothing to prevent graft, although I do not say that that is the object that the right hon. gentleman has in view. I am only pointing out that graft will be possible under these conditions.
Outside of the great question of taking this money out of the country, and outside of the great constitutional question involved, the most serious matter for us in this Parliament to consider is that these vessels are being built without tender and without the ordinary safeguards which should be thrown around their construction. If you want any confirmation of our

fears in this regard I would like to call the attention of the House to some remarkable figures which have been given regarding the construction of these vessels. The British Admiralty told us in 1909 that a vessel of certain specifications would cost $11,162,000. My right hon. friend the Prime Minister told us on December 5 last that, from the information which he had received from the British Admiralty in October the same vessel would cost $11,750,000. My hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Hazen) comes down to this House in January and tells us that this same vessel will cost $13,056,000. The same vessel, on the same specification, under exactly the same conditions, built in the same country and by the same people in one year will cost us $11,162,000 and in another year $13,056,000. There is practically an increase of $2,000,000 on the same vessel. Yet, they tell us, in the face of figures like these, that there is no necessity of calling for tenders and that everything will be perfectly straight. Then again, coming down to comparative figures, let us take the Lion, the latest completed ship in the British navy; the Minister of Marine and Fisheries says that this vessel costs $11,421,000. This Navy League Annual, this red-book, which has been referred to as Britain's imminent danger, and which will be accepted by hon. gentlemen opposite as an authority, says that this vessel only cost $10,228,000, or a difference of $1,200,000. The right hon. Prime Minister told us in December that these three vessels that it is proposed to build would cost $35,000,000 and the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries, two or three months afterwards stated in answer to the hon. member for Welland (Mr. German) that they might cost $39,000,000. In three months the price had gone up by $4,000,000. What does all this mean? Are the Government preparing the people of Canada to sign a contract for the construction of these vessels at a figure away above what the ordinary cost in Great Britain would be? If that"be the case what is going to become of the difference? That is the question. If these vessels can be built in Great Britain for $11,000,000 and we are going to pay $13,000,000 for them, what becomes of the $2,000,000? Of course the hon. Minister of Public Works (Mr. Rogers), not being the Minister of Naval Service, does not know anything about it, but probably he has been in the Cabinet when this has been discussed. But there is in that enough to make the ordinary ratepayer in Canada suspicious, especially when my right hon. friend refuses to do this work in the ordinary business lawful way in Canada and when he is compelled to get a special statute passed to get around the provisions of the law which requires that all public works shall be built by public tender or contract.
I do not want to elaborate this matter or take up any more of the time of the House.
I discussed it in the committee stage of the Bill, and I felt it to be my duty to bring it to the attention of the House at the present time. I have given the law and the facts sufficiently to show that there is grave cause for apprehension, that there is grave cause for alarm because the difference between the figures which my hon. friends are now saying these vessels will cost and what they said they would cost when they introduced this Bill in December ought to call for investigation and is in itself sum-cient ground for demanding that some protection shall be thrown around the expenditure of the public money of Canada. There is no reason that my right hon. friend can urge for not calling for tenders. There are seven, eight or nine big firms building vessels in Great Britain and they will all tender; they are all anxious to do business. Let them all tender, let my right hon. friend get prices, such as we had when we attempted to build a navy in Canada. We had tenders from all the principle ship-building firms in Great Britain and we were able to tell to a dollar what these vessels would cost. We were able to compare one tender with another and we were able to say whether the lowest tender was a reasonable price or not. We were not compelled to say that we would take this tender or that because it was the lowest but we had an opportunity of comparing all the tenders and of seeing^ what one price was as compared with another. That is an advantage that the right hon. gentleman would have if he would call for tenders. He should have tenders from seven or eight different firms in England and then, if he wants to go to the government dockyards, he will be able to know what the proper price should be and he will know whether he is paying more for these vessels than he ought to. In the interest of the Government of the country, as well as for the protection of the public at large, he should adopt the plan of calling for public tenders for the ships and they should not be built except by contract founded upon public tender, giving the contract to the lowest tenderer unless there is some very good reason for acting to the contrary. Therefore I move, seconded by Hon. Mr. Murphy;
That the Bill be not now read a third time, but that it be referred back to the Committee of the Whole with instructions to amend it by adding the following words to section 6: ' provided, however, that all the work executed under this Act shall be by contract awarded upon public tender.'

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I need not go over the same ground that I traversed on a previous occasion in reply to some observations of my hon. friend from iCarleton (Mr. Carvell), which were directed to the

same question as that which he has brought to the attention of the House this afternoon. Whether or not the section of the Public Works Act which he has quoted would relate to the construction of ships, I have already stated that the principle of tender and contract, which is a very good principle, is one from which we do not propose to depart in connection with the construction of these ships. I brought to the attention of the committee the possibility that one or more of these ships might be built in a royal dockyard. For that reason I did not think it advisable to add any such clause to the Bill. It seems to me that there is no disagreement between the two sides of the House as to the principle which ought to be followed by a government in respect to a matter of this kind.
The hon. gentleman drew a very alarming picture as to the increase in cost, as stated by the Admiralty. We are not responsible for their statements in that regard. We have given their statements to the House precisely as they were given to us. It is undoubtedly true that within a period of two or three months the cost of a battleship or armoured cruiser of the most modern and powerful type has increased, according to the statements of the Admiralty. I brought that fact to the attention of the House. I have no reason to believe that the estimate given to us on either one occasion or the other was incorrect. My hon. friend and every other member will realize that there are a great many considerations which might bring about that increased cost within a very short time. There was a certain increase in wages during that period, and I believe also that during the last six months or a year there has been a considerable increase in the cost of material.* Besides all that, there are other considerations which might increase the cost of a ship described in terms such as those I used when I addressed the House on the 5th of December last. I spoke of a battleship or armoured cruiser of the most modern and powerful type. Anyone having the slightest acquaintance with modern construction understands that the types of these ships are continually changing.

My right hon. friend
has evidently misunderstood me, because I was referring to the same vessel and the same type, the cost of which increased from $11,162,000 to $13,056,000.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
My hon. friend has not appreciated my point. It might very well be said that a battleship or armoured cruiser of the most modern and powerful type in September or October, 1911, would not, after new designs had been brought out in December or January, be
Mr. BORDEN.
then a battleship or armoured cruiser of the most modern and powerful type.
It is the same ship, the same type.	[DOT]

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: If I cannot make myself clear to the hon. gentleman by the language which I have used, I am sorry, inasmuch as the design, the size, the speed, the armour, of a battleship of the most modern and powerful type, may change within a period of three or four months, it is perfectly apparent that the price may change correspondingly, and must do so.
That would not be the same type of vessel.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My hon. friend will have to make the best he can of my language.
All right.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I am afraid I cannot
make it any clearer. It is clear to my mind. I hope it is clear to the minds of hon. gentlemen.
If this Bill had been passed on the 12th day of December last, when the right hon. the leader of the Opposition made his speech, and had been immediately assented to by the Senate, and if designs had been prepared within three or four weeks of that date, those designs might be in certain respects of a different character from designs for a battleship or armoured cruiser prepared in July, August or Sep^ tember next. The armour might be of a different character, the armament might be less powerful and the speed might be less than in the later designs. That reason among others might account to some extent for any increase in the cost.
There is absolutely no intention on the part of the Government to depart from well recognized principles in regard to the construction of these ships. We hope to utilize the expert knowledge of the British Admiralty, and we shall see to it that these ships are built with every possible safeguard to protect the public interest that is applied to the construction of ships for His Majesty's Government in the United Kingdom.

The right hon. gentleman says that there is no intention upon the part of the Government to depart from the well recognized principle of advertising for tenders. If that is the case, why not accept the amendment of the hon. member? Surely there can be no objection to the Government putting that in the Bill and settling by positive declaration what the right hon. gentleman says the Government intend to do. I cannot quite understand the philosophy of the right hon. gentleman when he says: We do not intend to depart from well recognized prin-

ciples of public tender. If he does not, all the amendment of my hon. friend from Carleton (Mr. Carvell) Says is that there shall be put in this Bill a clause declaring that the Government shall advertise for tenders.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I have explained to my hon. friend that it is quite possible that one or more of these ships may be built in a royal dockyard. If so, they would be built under every possible safeguard that protects the public interest in respect of the construction of such ships in the United Kingdom for His Majesty the King. Under those circumstances and in view of the declarations that I have made to the House, it seems to me there ought not to be any idea or suggestion on the part of hon. gentlemen opposite that well recognized principles will be departed from. They will not be departed from.

My right hon. friend
may not be here. These ships will take three years to build. Some other king may reign in Israel.
If my right hon. friend found that he could have a vessel built moTe cheaply in a private dockyard than in a royal dockyard, would he prefer building it in the latter?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
My hon. friend will
realize that in a case of this kind, where very great interests are in question, and where we have not the knowledge or the experience that is possessed by the great organization that exists in the United Kingdom, we should do well, it seems to me, to be guided by that expert advice under which the greatest navy in the world has been built up, and built up without a breath of suspicion having been cast upon the expenditure of public money in that work of construction. With that statement, it does seem to me the House ought to be absolutely reassured. I have never heard any question as to the proper expenditure of money for naval construction in the United Kingdom. I am not very familiar with that matter, and may be speaking without warrant upon the actual facts; but, so far as my knowledge goes, no question as to the proper expenditure of those funds has ever been raised. We propose, as we - have not the knowledge and experience, to be guided by the knowledge and experience acquired in centuries of shipbuilding, and to have these ships built under the direction and with the advice of the Admiralty, seeking all the advantages which come to us from the experience and knowledge which they have in these matters. It is undoubtedly true, so far as my knowledge-limited knowledge, I admit-will enable me to judge, that in naval construction Great Britain leads the
world, and has lead the world for a great many years. It seems to me that by placing ourselves in the hands of the Admiralty, and adopting the safeguards which they have, adopted and of which they make use, we shall maintain and safeguard the public interest in this country in regard to naval construction.

The right hon. gentleman has not answered the question.
