speakeroldname: Mr. W. F. CARROLL (South Cape Breton) :
speechtext:
If the members on the Government side do not agree with me in the motion which I now desire to make, I think there is at least one ground upon which they will see eye to eye with me, and that is, at the present stage of this measure, that I am in order in moving an amendment. The expression of my views on this occasion will necessarily be brief, because when this Bill was being considered by the Com-
Mr. CARVlECDL.
mittee of the Whole House, I gave my views on the matter and the reasons why at that time I attempted to move an amendment to Bill No. 21, intituled the Naval Aid Act. I shall now briefly outline, as reasons for moving this amendment, the views I presented at that time. Before coming to that, however, I desire to say that I have in no wise lost any of the strength of my opposition to the general terms of the Naval Aid Act as it at present stands. I have held and still hold that the proper course to be pursued by the Canadian Government, as representing the people of this country, is the organization of a Canadian navy, the ships of which shall be built in this country, out of our own material and by our own workmen and artisans. I am no less strong in that opinion to-day, even though I am moving this amendment. However, it seems that the Government do not intend to withdraw the present measure _ and take a course which would give the industries and workmen and artisans of this country the great stimulus which the expenditure of $35,000,000 would necessarily afford to them. The Government of the day have given reasons why they have determined to bring this legislation into effect; they have given their reasons for not living up to the Naval Service Act of 1910. To my mind, the reasons given by the present Administration do not seem sound. I do not think anv man who has any grasp upon public opinion, eitheT in this country or in the British Empire at large, will say that at the present stage there	is	an emergency	of any
kind within the British Empire. It seems to me that the idea that an emergency exists, which was the principal reason given by the present Administration for the bringing down of this Bill, has been absolutely dispelled. It seems to me that the people of Canada are absolutely aware of the fact that there is no such emergency, and that there is at the present time not even a need for this Government to send thirty-five million Canadian dollars to the Mother Country. The only good effect it will have on the Motherland will be to stimulate the great ship-building industry of England, and make it greater than it is. I gave the other day my reason for having reached this conclusion, and those reasons I based upon information found on the pages of one of the most prominent of the great English dailies, the London Times. It was stated that there was no reason in the world to doubt the capacity of the Canadian people to enter upon the construction of ships, but, said the Times: If they do enter upon ship-building, thus creating a great industry in Canada, they will lessen and decrease the value of the ship-building industry of Great Britain.' There are certain journals in this country which have

a certain influence over Canadian public opinion, and when one in his capacity as a public servant desires to bring his views before this Parliament or before the country, they accuse him of selfish motives. I give all due credit to the opinions of every hon. gentleman of this House, but when those journals-and I have to point out that the Montreal Star is the greatest sinner in this regard-undertake to lecture the members of this House and say that the reason why hon. gentlemen express themselves as being desirous that a shipbuilding industry shall be established in this country is because they are actuated by selfish motives. I may tell them that they are not the moulders in its entirety of public opinion in this country. We are entitled to our own opinions, and when hon. gentlemen are sent to this House with a mandate from the people on a policy of shipbuilding in Canada in pursuance of the Naval Service Act, it ill behooves any newspaper in this country to say that their opinions are based upon selfish motives. You may call it selfishness if you will, but I say that there is an opinion to-day, in my part of the country at least, that it would be in the best interests of Nova Scotia, of Canada and of the Empire at large if the terms of the Naval Service Act of 1910 were put into effect. It has been said that this Act was a separatist Act, inasmuch as this Parliament had control over the actions of whatever naval force might spring up under its terms. Let me point out that under the present Bill as it stands the Governor in Council has that power; the Governor in Council may withdraw the ships at any time. What would happen if during a great conflict in any part of the British Empire, a majority of the Council were composed of the Nationalist party? That is not an impossibility, and, on that score at least, the Naval Service Act is worthy of more favourable consideration than the present proposed legislation. The Conservative party in this country have since 1867, always boasted that they are the friends of the great industries of this country. Many years ago they introduced and passed a tariff Act in this Parliament. This Act had a two-fold object. The principal object was that great industries might be established and flourish under the application of its provisions. The second object was that a revenue might be obtained to carry on the public business of the country. Since the inception of that national policy the Conservative party in this country have always boasted that they are the friends of the industries; they have always boasted that the industries received a great stimulus under this national policy. I am not going to argue that point. If that is their desire; if that be their ambition, here is a chance for them to make good their assertions and professions in that regard. Here is a chance to encourage
a great industry in this country; here is a chance to add a stimulus to the steel and lumber industries of Canada. Here is an opportunity of giving a stimulus to the nickle industry of this country. If, therefore, hon. gentlemen opposite are the friends of industry in this country,, they surely must accept the amendment which I propose to move to the Naval Aid Act. On what ground can the members of the Government vote against this amendment? If they vote against this amendment, they are voting against certain industries in this country, they are voting against the workmen and the artisans who gain their livelihood in these industries. Does their loyalty carry them so far that it requires of them to decry those three industries that I have mentioned in order, not to overcome an emergency which they say exists in the British Empire, but to help out the great shipping industry of Great Britain. As well might this Government and the Railway Department of this Government, when they require an engine or a box car or any other equipment for the Intercolonial, send over to the contractors of Great Britain and tell them that, in view of the fact that we are loyal to the British Empire, that we want to build it up, we will send our money over there and allow the contractors of Great Britain to build all the necessary cars for the government railways of Canada. What would be the result of this policy if it was carried to its logical conclusion? The result might be that some time in the future some person in Great Britain could arise and say that the railway facilities of Great Britain were not sufficient to carry their soldiers to war and they would ask this Government to send over a few million dollars in order to build some more railways in Great Britain or it might transpire that in some other part of the Empire somebody, having if you will selfish motives, or, if you will, good motives, would require the expenditure of a large amount of money for any public work or any great undertaking. I say it would be just as sound for the Government to do that as to do what they anticipate and intend to do under this present Act. It would be a great thing, and I do not think it would interfere with this Bill as it stands, if at least $10,000,000 or $11,000,000 of this $35,000,000 were spent in this country. If we cannot have it all, let us have an expenditure of $10,000,000 or $11,000,000. About one-third of the cost of a battleship is made up of the materials which go into it. If the cost of those battleships will be in the vicinity of $33,000,000 or $35,000,000, and if the material at least were procured in this country, it would mean the expenditure of something like $11,000,000 in the great industries I have mentioned. Is not that a matter of some moment for the present

Government to take into consideration? We were sent to this Parliament first of all in the interests of the Canadian people, and I ask the right hon. leader of the Government and hon. gentlemen opposite, is it in the interest of the Canadian people, of Canadian workmen and Canadian industry, that $11,000,000 which could be spent in this country under the Naval Service Act as it stands, should be sent out and spent across the Atlantic. I think there are reasons for reflection and consideration on this matter. The question was hurriedly discussed the other day and I shall not dwell upon it longer but, having regard to the welfare of certain Canadian industries and having regard to the welfare of Canadian workmen and artisans, I beg leave to move the following:
That the Bill be not now read the third time but that the same be referred back to Committee of the Whole House for the purpose of adding the following as clause 7.
Whenever practicable, in the construction of the ships provided for in this Act, the constructors or builders shall be bound to accept steel and other material produced in Canada.	i	i i j

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. L. BORDEN (Prime Minister) :
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council

speechtext:
It was not my intention, Mr. Speaker, to take part in the discussion on the third lecture of this Bill, but I am induced to say a few words by reason of a remark made this morning by the hon. member for Welland (Mr. German). Before submitting his amendment, the hon. member for Welland has declared that he thought he was expressing the opinion of all the members of the Opposition in asking the Government to vote each year a certain sum of money for building dreadnoughts in England, under the control of the government of Canada.
For my part, I object to having dreadnoughts built in England, whichever mode is adopted, either with the money voted in a lump sum, or divided into three parts so as to form the 35 millions necessary.
I object to such a policy, for two reasons : In the first place, because England has no need whatever of those three dreadnoughts; and, secondly, because Canada feels that need still less.
The Prime Minister has stated on several occasions that such a policy of contribution would not be a permanent policy. He has also often reminded us that it would take from 25 to 50 years to build up a Canadian navy. He qualifies to-day his declaration by saying: A navy equal to the British navy.
I do not think that anybody will sustain in this House that Canada must build up a navy which would be equal to the British



navy. It would take every able-bodied man in Canada to man such a fleet, and even then it would be necessary to resort to foreign help.
I am a farmer and a trader since twenty years, and I cannot help asking myself how it is that so much time is consumed in discussing a business question.
With respect to the Naval policy, adopted in 1909 by the Liberal party, with the cooperation of the Opposition of the time, I have not deviated from the same point, and in my opinion we should stick to it.
Dreadnoughts might perhaps be necessary in 25 or 50 years from now, but before that we should begin by building smaller ships, so as to form a fleet, and when that fleet will have been built and will form two units, one being stationed on the Atlantic and the other on the Pacific, then we might think of adding a dreadnought to each one of those units.
Mr. Churchill, who has been so conspicuous in this House-and Heaven knows how hard it has been for the Opposition to have his letter brought up to light-has declared that we, Canadians, are incapable, that our efforts are scarcely worth anything, and that, in fact, we constitute a negligible quantity. I must say that all that trash has not roused me too much. When I spoke of it to my electors, they were not more agitated than I had been. In fact they would rather be deemed an incapable lot of people and have the privilege to keep their money. The man who keeps his money to himesif can always use it as he sees it. That was the policy adopted by the Japanese and the Australians. Have not the Japanese shown themselves to be clever enough to build their own navy, of which the power is to-day acknowledged everywhere? And the Australians, with a population much less numerous than ours, are also imbued with the same spirit.
I must say, then, to those hon. gentlemen opposite: Don't be in_ such a hurry; wait until we are in a position to do something.
I find it very strange that those hon. gentlemen, who were all in favour of a referendum in 1910, and among whom there are some who have again voted in favour of a referendum, are now supporting the policy of the Government. All the members of the Province of Quebec used to declare that they were opposed to any navy and to any contribution, without a referendum. I am surprised that those hon. gentlemen do not force the Government to appeal to the people. The three French Canadian ministers have declared themselves in favour of a referendum; they have stated that nothing would be done without appealing first to the people. Where are they all to-day? I can see one, at the present moment, in this House. He must not assuredly, be opposed Mr. LANCTOT.
to a referendum. He has not, surely, repudiated what he has advocated before the electors of the Province of Quebec. How then explain that he now remains silent on that point? All those conversations lead me to believe that the policy of contribution inaugurated this year will be kept up in the future. I have always fought that policy in my country, and I cannot approve it to-day. That is the policy of the tory-jingoes: one king, one empire, one fleet. That was the policy advocated by the Prime Minister, when he returned from England last summer.
I greatly fear that we will never have a Canadian navy, and that we will on the contrary have a policy of permanent contribution, in proportion to the population, as an aid to the Imperial Navy. How is it that you, who were so much opposed to any expense for military purposes, do not now object to all that?
There are vague rumours of elections. Those very ministers who have not kept the promises made to their electors do not want an appeal to the people. Better wait two or three years, and then a good many of those gentlemen will have disappeared from the political arena; some will be called to the Bench, and the others will take whatever plums are offered them. They will not be hard to please, so long as they do not appear again before their electors. Efforts will thus be made to take them away, as much as possible, from the Province of Quebec, and have their places taken by others who will not be implicated as they were. Such is the compromise arrived at, between the Prime Minister and those hon. gentlemen.	'	_
I pity those who will have to remain to face the music before their electors, because short work will then be made of them and they will have richly deserved their fate.
I will not delay the House any longer. Being a farmer, and representing a county exclusively agricultural where there are nevertheless a few workingmen, I wanted to protest once more against that legislation which takes us backwards 60 or 70 years, in asking us to pay tribute to England. I wanted my protestation entered in the Hansard and to say that, if we must do something, it should be for the protection of our shores and our commerce, and all for Canada and only for Canada.
I agree with the member for Cape-Breton, Who, by his amendment, has asked the Government to decree that, so far as possible, only Canadian material should be used in the construction of those three dreadnoughts.

Mr. Speaker, five months
ago the. Government, as the result of the examination and consideration of condi-

tions affecting this Empire and Canada's relations thereto, submitted a proposal to this Parliament and asked for its approval. After a long period of discussion and controversy we have now come to the final hours of the debate when every member of this House, representing as he does thousands of Canadian citizens, will be asked to exercise his responsibility by his vote signifying his approval or disapproval of this measure. We all admit that this is a deep and a grave responsibility. It is not my wish or intention to delay the House at this time at any length at all, but I have listened, as many other hon. members have to most of the arguments which have been placed before the House by various members and, as I have not as yet spoken at all upon this question, I trust that the House will pardon a few brief remarks. If I perhaps do not confine myself to answering my hon. friend's amendment I feel that you, Mr. Speaker, and the members of the House will pardon me in this case.
We all agree, I think, that it is a profoundly regrettable fact that this matter, which so vitally affects our common citizenship, our world relationship and our national future, should be plunged into the strife of party politics. I know that we shall not agree as to who shall bear the responsibility for plunging it there. After all we are perhaps too close to the theatre of conflict to ourselves have a very clear vision of that point, but it is certainly true that our judges will be the millions of our fellow subjects who have sent us here as their trustees. Then further I might say, and I venture to think that there will not be much dissent from the remark, that no equally great question was ever laid before any Parliament in terms characterized by loftier patriotism, greater freedom from party sentiment or deeper sincerity than those used by my right hon. friend the Prime Minister (Mr. Borden) on the 5th day of December last. If the manner of that message was above reproach, we on this side of the House feel also that its matter was. Six years ago, at the Imperial conference, the Prime Minister of Great Britain, in speaking of the problems of Empire used these words:
Let me ask you to realize what our position is. Forty-three millions of people in those two small islands bearing on our shoulders-I do not complain of it-this burden, we are quite willing to sustain-the whole weight of the debt which has been incurred in the formation and development of this Empire, bearing also the cost, at any rate, the great bulk of the cost-of the Imperial defence not only of these islands, but of the whole Empire in all its parts.
I think that no member of this House will dispute the truth of that statement. Canada has presented in the past a spectacle unparalleled as far as I know in the history of the world-a young, strong, growing country prosecuting year after year the development of its own resources, building up its own industrial and social fabric, absolutely unhindered by a thought of external interference solely and simply by the fact that between us and any conceivable trouble from the outside stood the power and might of the navy of Great Britain.
It would only be wearisome, nor is it necessary to discuss the much discussed question of whether the absolute supremacy of that navy is in any way threatened or jeopardized by naval and military developments in other parts of the world? The right hon. gentleman (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) and the party he leads have assumed that no such possible danger exists. Some hon-members have indeed gone very far, like the-hon. member from South Renfrew (Mr. Graham), who has asserted that Great Britain not only is not in danger but never will be. It is true, and there is perhaps some little solace in this, that my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition has said very positively that if England is ever in danger, or even on trial, he would be the first to go to the people and call them to assist with all their might. When the clock has struck, however, and the day of trial is at hand, my right hon. friend will be too late in his preparations and his appeals.
We believe on our side of the House that evidences sufficient have been given by those best able to give them that the peace and security of this Empire will be best assured by immediate strengthening of its naval forces. No truer word has been spoken than that by the great Imperial soldier, Lord Roberts, when he said that this Empire is always practically defenceless beyond its first line. The Bill now before this House is for the purpose of strengthening the first line of defence, and whatever may be the views of hon. members as to the gradual construction of naval forces in this country, we hold on this side of the House that our first duty is to provide immediate and effective aid in the way proposed by the Prime Minister. My right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition, and those behind him, have spent very many words in denouncing as unpatriotic and un-Canadian the expenditure of money for the construction of three battleships for the strengthening of British naval supremacy.
I will not go into that argument, but I would point out to him that on February 3, 1910 when he was talking about the financial assistance extended by England to other nations to strengthen them during the Napoleonic war, he referred to Napoleon's description of England as a 'nation of shopkeepers ' and said:
For Canada, for my country, I would de-1 sire no better title than to be called a nation of shopkeepers and to be able to supply the! sinews of war.

in this House on the 7th of February last which. I think, is eminently true:
The question of our naval services and coast defence should be carefully studied and the advice and assistance of the best experts obtained. I sometimes think that the less a man knows about a question like this the more apt he is to express a very strong opinion about it.
And I would commend to attention one other passage in that lion, gentleman's speech, as follows:
The question for Canada to decide is not the definition of the word ' emergency '; but what is our duty? Is it not clear that our duty is to give every assistance within our power to Great Britain at the present time?
I do not wish to detain the House by speaking longer. We believe on this side of the House-and I am confident that I speak for the people I represent in that far western province-that this measure should receive the cordial sanction of the House, and that it will and does command the strongest sympathy and support of the Canadian people. One of the hon. members opposite speaking in this debate quoted a passage from Joseph Howe. Whatever differences of opinion there may be as to Mr. Howe's political career he stands in the memory of us all as a strong, big-hearted Oanadian of large views and lofty patriotism. Perhaps the House will permit me, in closing, to quote one memorable passage from the utterances of Joseph Howe, this being a speech on the Organization of Empire delivered on the 11th of March, 1854:
In no vain spirit do I wish also that the sentiments which I am about to utter, might be heard and pondered, not only as they will be by those who inhabit half this continent, but by members of the British Parliament, by Imperial statesmen, by the counsellors who stand around, and by the gracious sovereign who sits upon the Throne. Perhaps this may not be. Yet I believe that the day is not distant when our sons, standing in our places, trained in the enjoyment of public liberty by those who have gone before them, and compelled to be statesmen by the throbbing of their British blood, and by the necessities of their position, will be heard across the Atlantic; and will utter to each other, and to all the world, sentiments which to-day, Mr. Chairman, may fall with an air of novelty upon your ear, I am not sure, Sir, that even out of this discussion may not arise the spirit of union and elevation of thought that may lead North America to oast aside her Colonial habiliments, to put on national aspects, to assert national claims and pre pare to assume national obligations.
And he closed with this fine thought:
Come what may, I do not hesitate to express the hope that from this date she will aspire to consolidation as an integral portion of the realm of England, or assert her claims to a national existence.
Mr. BURRElLE.
It is in the belief that the Bill now before the House makes for that consolidation that I shall vote for it firmly convinced that in doing so I am expressing the mature conviction of the people whom I represent and am doing my duty and theirs.

When the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Carroll) moved his amendment I did not intend to say a word in connection with it, but the speech of the Prime Minister and the observations of others to which it has given rise brought to my mind the necessity of making some reply. At that stage I did not know that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Burrell) was to make a speech. I must say that in my judgment the speech of that hon. gentleman has nothing in common with the amendment before the Chair, and I submit that, according to the pronounced rulings-[DOT] and I suppose proper rulings-which we have had from Your Honour frequently and recently that the last motion before the Chair is the one to which hon. members must address themselves, the hon. minister was not in order. But, as he has had his little speech in course of preparation from day to day, I suppose, since the introduction of this Bill, and as it is clear it was not ready until now, far be it from me to place any obstacles in the way of the hon. gentleman reciting his ' Mary had a little lamb ' before this House. If anything were needed to show that no undue time has been taken up in the discussion of this Bill, if any evidence were necessary to absolutely and forever refute the argument put forth by hon. gentlemen opposite that too much time has been taken up, and that obstruction has been offered to the progress of this Bill, that evidence is furnished by the speech of the Minister of Agriculture. That hon. gentleman, while a member of the Government, who felt that he had important information to give, who felt that there were high principles that he wished to emphasize, that there were grand ideas of Empire in his heart and head of which the people of the country should be made aware before they were called upon to pass judgment on this Bill, it is only now that he is prepared to finish the discussion on the Government side and give us this speech. Where, then, is the obstruction, where is the time mis-spent on this side, when the Government have not been ready themselves until this moment to have the country properly pronounce upon this subject? I am sure that no other minister of the Crown, and no member supporting the Government would dare to say that the time to pronounce upon this measure had arrived when we had not before us the opinion of the hon. gentleman who has last addressed the House. Nor do we know that some other of the hon. gentlemen who adorn my

right hon. friend's Cabinet may not be maturing speeches which must be heard before this matter is concluded. I was told that possibly we may get some opinions on that navy question from the Minister of Inland Revenue (Mr. Nantel). I have ithe greatest regard for the Minister of Inland Revenue. We sat close together in this House some years ago when hon. gentlemen who now support the Government were on this side of the House, and I learned to have a great deal of respect for that hon. gentleman. I remember distinctly that when' he was sitting on this side of the House he made a very pronounced speech upon the naval question. If the hon. minister would make that speech again, I am of the opinion that he would make matters Tather uncomfortable for the Prime Minister and those who sit behind him. But I take it for granted that my hon. friend the Minister of Inland Revenue has seasoned himself to his surroundings, and that he has used his political padlock to shut off the conveyance of any information that might be embarrassing to the Prime Minister.
If there is one point more than another that is worthy of notice in the speech of the hon. member who has just taken his seat, the Minister of Agriculture, it is the emphasis he laid" upon the fact that the Prime Minister has an overwhelming mandate from the people of Canada with regard to this matter. I submit that, if we understand aright what the getting of a mandate from the people on any specific question really means, a mandate is obtained only after due deliberation upon the issue by the people. When the judgment of the people is then obtained, it should be regarded as a mandate with regard to that question. The province of Nova Scotia is the native province of the Prime Minister, and I submit that so far as Nova Scotia is concerned, hon. gentlemen opposite have no mandate with regard to this question of naval construction, because it was not an issue in the last election. The Minister of Agriculture is therefore speaking entirely aside from the question and without due regard to the facts when he says that the Government can go forward with this because they have a mandate from the people. They have nothing of the kind. As to the province of Quebec whatever mandate they have from that province, it is absolutely and diametrically opposed to the course now being taken by the Government.

Was my hon. friend
not in the House when the hon. member for South Cape Breton (Mr. Carroll) said that he was elected largely upon the policy of a Canadian-built navy?
That was certainly the policy of Sir Wilfrid Laurier; it was well understood in that province.
The hon. gentleman has said that the naval question was not an issue in the province of Nova Scotia.

If there was an issue
in regard to that matter, it certainly had reference to the question as to whether the ships should be built, and whether any part of their construction would be carried on, in the town of Sydney. If, in his younger days, the hon. member for Portage la Prairie had been promised a pair of boots by his father, the question as to whether or not he should buy them would not be subject to decision; the only matter at issue would be as to which of two stores he should purchase them-the matter of his getting the boots was settled. So far as the province of Nova Scotia is concerned, the
Suestion as to whether we should have a anadian navy according to the programme outlined by Sir Wilfrid Laurier was settled; it was simply a question as to where .the ships should be built and whether we would get any share of that building in Sydney.
Is that the hon. gentleman's conception of Empire?

It is not always wise
to pay a great deal of attention to the hon. member for Peterborough (Mr. Burnham). As graver questions are now before us, I leave my hon. friend to deal with such matters as theology, the French language, and the question as to whether we are married or not. I propose to confine my observations in answer to my hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture largely to this matter of the obtaining of a mandate from the people. Mr. Speaker, like those of
my fellow members who have addressed themselves to the third reding of this Bill, I Rave no intention of re-opening the main issue which has been discussed for such a long time, though not too long, I am sure. But. as far as we are concerned on this side of the House, the discussion was closed on Saturday last at two o'clock in the morning when the rules of closure were applied against us.	On the present occasion I rise,
as I have said, not to discuss the Bill, but simply to offer a last protest- Not that I have any expectation that anything that may be said by me on this occasion can in any way affect the decision soon to be recorded by the majority. Yet this vote settles nothing: the question Temainis, and the result will simply complicate the problem of defence. The question must come up again for consideration, and it is fitting that we should lay down the landmarks which should guide our course not only at this time but in future years.
In many quarters surprise is expressed at the strenuousness of the opposition which we have offered to this measure. In this there is no cause for surprise; indeed, there would have been cause for surprise if we had failed to do what we have done. When a measure of this importance, a measure which is at variance with the historic traditions that we have followed in this country since Confederation, is introduced into this House, the people have a right to expect that their rulers will treat them with frankness and candour, will show them whither they are led, and above all will see that the public is consulted before the final decision is reached. On all these counts the Government have been remiss, unfaithful and delinquent. We arraign them before the people on all these grounds. The first indictment which I present against them is that the very reason upon which this measure is based has absolutely no foundation in fact.
When, some few months ago, in the earliest days of this session, members who support the Government were told that there was an emergency in the affairs of Great Britain and that Great Britain

should receive the assistance of this country, they did not suspect, I am sure, that before the last vote would be taken they would have in their hands absolute evidence of the falsity of the assertion which was then made. When they were told that there was an emergency and that the condition of things which prevailed in England required that immediately the people of Canada should contribute the sum of $35,000,000 to procure three of the largest battleships which money could buy or science devise, they would have seen at once what a cold mockery it was, if there was such a danger, that we should send three empty ships into the firing line. But they are easily led away from the truth who are desirous of being led away from the truth, and our hon. friends were ready to believe, and in fact did believe, that there was such an emergency; and we witnessed a climax of enthusiasm when the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Foster) summarized the situation in these graphic words:
From what quarter is England menaced? From Asia, no; from Africa, no; from America, no; where is her menace to-day? It is in Europe, and if combinations of powers, or if any power in Europe aims a spear at her heart, be the aim taken in Europe or elsewhere, that is where my shield and helm ought to be, to ward off the pointed dart and to prevent the death that otherwise would come.
This was certainly graphic language, and well do I remember the enthusiasm with which it was greeted. But the unreality of these words was shown at a not very distant day when the First Lord of the Admiralty stated that these ships which would be contributed by Canada were not to be placed on the firing line, but were to be placed under the shadow of the rock of Gibraltar.
What a fall was there for these staunch Imperialists who had dreamed by night and thought by day that their helm and shield would be there to ward off the blow! But what a triumph for the Nationalists whose souls had been tortured for so many years by the expectation that their sons might be called away from their homes to be disembowelled on board these ships ! The Nationalists to-day can rest in peace, they can slumber without trouble, because no one will be disembowelled upon these ships so long as they are under the shadow of the rock of Gibraltar and have the protection of the guns of the citadel. If these ships are to be named after Canadian celebrities, I would suggest to my right hon. friend the Prime Minister (Mr. Borden) three names which would be quite in accordance with the fitness of things-Pelletier, Nantel and Coderre.
But there is more than that. We proposed a counter policy, which was that we should continue the policy which had been adopted in 1909, that we should have a naval service of our own; and we showed that this policy was suggested by the very facts disclosed in the memorandum of the British Admiralty. That memorandum stated that on account of the augmentation of the navies of European powers, the Admiralty had been forced to withdraw their naval forces from distant seas and concentrate them in European waters. Our policy was that we should have two fleet units, one on the Atlantic and one on the Pacific, to take the places of the British squadrons which had been removed from those waters. But the rejoinder which we received was to the effect that the contribution was an emergency contribution, an extraordinary contribution, to be made on account of a sudden condition of things which had arisen, and that we therefore could not do anything along the line of a permanent policy such as we proposed. As the discussion went on, my hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Mr. White), whom we all regret not to see among us to-day, thought that he had discovered a paramount argument against our policy. He found that argument in a speech of Mr. Churchill, the First Lord of the Admiralty, delivered on the 31st March last, in which Mr. Churchill made use of the following language:
I ask the House seriously:	Is it not unwise for some people on one side of the House to say that the Canadian ships are redundant, superfluous and an unnecessary burden -(Hon. members: No)-and is it not equally unwise for other people on the other side to say that they ought to he redundant, superfluous, and an unnecessary burden. Both these views seem to me to he equally wrong and equally harmful to our interests, and 1 must repeat that the Canadian ships are absolutely necessary for the whole world defence of the British Empire from the end of 1915, or from the beginning of 1916 onwards.
I have never disguised the fact that I am an admirer of the young First Lord of the Admiralty. I have read some of his books, I have read some of his speeches, I have listened to some others, and on every occasion I, like everybody else, could not but marvel at his variety of gifts, his power of expression, his remarkable faculty of dramatically marshalling facts and ideas-in short, his versatility. On this occasion the one quality which was conspicuous was not the power of speech, not the faculty of dramatic expression, but rather his versatility, because we had not up to that time heard any such language on the part of the young First Lord of the Admiralty. Mr. Churchill, on the contrary, on every occasion had told us that the naval forces of England were adequate for any emergency that might arise; that England did

1001&
not need assistance from any quarter; that any assistance that might be given her by any of the young nations of the Empire would be welcome; but that, if that assistance did not come or could not come, Britain would face all perils that might come. This was indeed a strong argument to confirm the view represented by the Government that England was in need of assistance from Canada, and that the ships which were offered by Canada would be required by the year 1915.
There is something more than this. My hon. friend the Minister of Finance did not give us the whole of the quotation. If he had gone further, another story would have been unfolded. My hon. friend from St. Antoine (Mr. Ames) told us a few days ago that he would give the whole of the quotation from the speech of Mr. Churchill which bore upon this point. My hon. friend made a quotation, which I shall read in its entirety in order to show him that he did not give the whole of the quotation, but left out something which has a material bearing upon the point at issue. He prefaced the quotation with the following remarks:
His remarks have been referred to by the hon. Minister of iFinance and several other members, but have never before been placed on ' Hansard ' in their entirety. He said that up to the year 1914 the 60 per cent standard had been provided for. Then he goes on to say:
Then comes the quotation:
That is quite sufficient for the year 1915, with which we are at present dealing, but, haying regard to the responsibilities of the British Empire both in the Pacific and in, the Mediterranean, and having regard in particular to the new development of forces in the Mediterranean, it is clear that thlei margin of strength available for the whole world service of the British Empire will not be sufficient after the first quarter of 1916 unless further steps are taken either by the dominions or by ourselves. From the point of view, the reality of the need of the three Canadian vessels can be well appreciated. They would raise the margin of the strength available for the general defence of the Empire, after the main need in home waters has been met, as follows: 1915, in the fourth quarter, 10;	1916, in the first quarter, 13;
in the second quarter, 8; in the third quarter, 8; in the fourth quarter, 10; 1917, in1 the first quarter 13, and so on, an average of 9 or 10 vessels available for the whole world service of the British Empire. That, in the absence of further developments in the Mediterranean or in the Pacific beyond what is now in prospect, would he sufficient. If, how-over, new developments took place of such a kind as to affect Admiralty problems, or if the Canadian ships were to miscarry for any reason, the situation would have to be reviewed. It is unnecessary at the present moment, and it would be premature for me to say any more on the subject. I have given the fullest information in my power to the House, and I hope I shall not he pressed to Sir WILFRID LAURIER.
add to it. I could not accede to such a re-: quest. It is necessary, however, to make-it clear that the three ships now under discussion in Canada are absolutely required from 1916 onwards for the whole world defence of the British Empire, apart altogether from the needs of Great Britain in home waters; that they will play a real part in the defence of the Empire; and that, if they fail, a gap will be opened to fill which further sacrifices will have to be -made without undue delay by others.	_	.
With these facts in view, I ask the House* seriously: Is it not unwise for some people* on one side of the House to say that thef Canadian ships are redundant, superfluous, and an unnecessary burden-(Hon. members:
' No.')-and it is equally unwise for other' people on the other side to say that they1 ought to be redundant, superfluous, and an unnecessary burden? Both these views seem to me to be equally wrong and equally harmful to our interests, and I must repeat that the Canadian ships are absolutely necessary for the -whole world defence of the British Empire from the end of 1915, or from the* beginning of 1916 onwards. The fact that- . they are necessary is no measure of thein value. Their value far exceeds the value of three ships. We can build three ships ourselves if necessary. Parliament has never refused to supply the money for that which res-possible ministers have considered necessary for the proper discharge of the responsibilities of the Crown. It is the fact of this great new nation coming forward with all its measureless strength and possibility, to testify to the enduring life of the British Empire that has already produced an impression throughout the world of more value than, many dreadnought ships, an impression which throughout the world conduces both to* the safety of this country and to the peace of the nations.
There my hon. friend stopped, after stating that he would give the whole quotation which bore upon this point. If he had continued, he would have read the following sentence, which comes immediately at the point where he left off:
From this point of view the difference in method which separates the proposal of Mr. Borden's Government from those of that far-seeing Imperial statesman, Sir Wilfrid Lau-rier, are not of vital importance.

Will the right hon. the
leader of the Opposition be good enough to continue the quotation?

Certainly. I will read not only the quotation, but my hon. friend's mind, which I understand perfectly well. My hon. friend wants me to read further in order to draw attention to this statement of Mr. Churchill:
The Admiralty have expressed their opinion, as it was our duty to do, as to which is the most convenient method and which method will be the most quick and helpful and will be most effective for the common good of the British Empire. But from a wider standard than any rwbich the Admiralty can occupy

the principle of Canada, coming forward for the world-wide naval defence of itlhe British Empire is of inestimable value, and that is tihe principle on which I understand Liberals and Conservatives in Canada are at one.
My hon. friend wants to draw my attention to the statement that the method which has been adopted by the Government of a contribution rather than of a Canadian navy is in accordance with the views of the Admiralty. The Admiralty have on all occasions pronounced their preference for a policy of contribution rather than for a policy of autonomous organization. I grant that willingly to my hon. friend; but we on this side of the House have told the Admiralty that, although they expressed that preference we would not have a system of direct contribution but would have an autonomous organization.
If my hon. friend will allow me, I will show him that this policy is the right policy; and, if he asks for authority, I will give him an authority which, I am sure, he will not question-an authority which he accepts on all occasions: the authority of the present Prime Minister of Canada. Since he is in the way of asking for quotations, I will ask him to send to the library and get a copy of the Debates of this House of the 29th of March, 1909. He will find there the speech of the present Prime Minister, then leader of the Opposition. I have not seen it for some time, but I am as certain as I am that I exist that in that speech my right hon. friend stated that the Admiralty had expressed a preference for a contribution, but that that system had been tried in Australia and had failed, and that he was in favour of a Canadian navy. This is the way the question stands, not only before the Canadian people, but before the whole Empire. We have been told again and again-it is the basis upon which this measure has been drafted-that the British Admiralty desired our contribution-that such a contribution was necessary for the safety of the Empire. But you have the testimony of Mr. Churchill that though he would prefer the one, yet the policy of Sir Wilfrid Laurier is just as acceptable as the policy of Mr. Borden. I have just this to say to my hon. friends on the other side, and not only to these hon. gentlemen but to the Canadian people, nay, to the wide Empire: that we on this side of the House are as ready to bear our burden, to discharge the duty which we owe to the Motherland as British subjects, as any others can be; but we want to do it in the manner which was adopted by all parties at one time, when this question was approached free from party bias-by the organization of a Canadian navy on lines compatible with the autonomy of Canada. And which of these two policies is preferred by gentlemen on the other side? With the
exception of tvro, every hon. gentleman supporting the Government who has opened his lips on this question has told us he was in favour of a Canadian naval service at some time or other. But they declare that they are in favour of the present policy because it is necessary on account of an emergency. But Mr. Churchill says that the policy which we propose will be as effective at the present time as the policy of the Government.
What more need I say; what more should I say? Is it not evident that we are more than vindicated by the language of Mr. Churchill? Is it not evident that it would have been better for the Government not to adopt an emergency policy when there is no emergency, but to follow the policy adopted in 1909 and 1910? I will say no more on that point, but I repeat that I believe I have fully vindicated our course by the quotation I have given of the speech of Mr. Churchill.
Perhaps I might sit down now without saying anything further. But it will not be amiss, I suppose, if I review some of the other grounds on which we find fault with the Bill now before the House. It has been stated and repeated, and repeated again, that we owe a debt of gratitude to Great Britain.
Hear, hear.

So say I.
I never said anything else; on the contrary, I have maintained that attitude everywhere; I have always maintained that attitude in my own province on all occasions and under all oircumstances. But I do not base that gratitude upon the ground on which it is based by some hon. gentlemen. When we are told that we owe a debt of gratitude to Great Britain, that we should vote $35,000,000 to Great Britain because Great Britain has lent us money to develop this country, this is to my mind nothing more than a purely childish argument. If Great Briatin were to receive a dreadnought from every one of the countries to which she had lent money, her harbours would be so filled with these ships that there would be no place for the present British fleet. Great Britain has investments in all the countries of the world. She has investments in the United States, in Mexico, in Chili, in Venezuela, in Brazil, in the Argentine-in fact, in all the countries on the continent of America. She has investments in all the countries of Europe; in Austria, in Italy, in Spain, in Portugal, even in France and Germany. Great Britain has investments in Japan, in China, in all the countries of Asia and Africa. She has loaned money to states, to provinces, to cities, to towns; she has loaned money to ship-building industries,

to railway companies, to industrial enterprises, to corporations, to individuals-to every man who came to her willing to pay the rates of interest and furnish good security. If Canada has received money on loan from Great Britain, it has not been because of sentiment, but simply because Canada could afford the security and could pay the interest. Let the rate of interest be lowered, or the security be found wanting, and at once the door will be closed against us. There are interests which a few years ago found the doors of every bank in Britain open to them, which to-day are received with coldness because their securities are not supposed to be as good as they were.
Nor do I admit that we owe gratitude to Great Britain because she spent money to defend this country. Sir, sovereignty implies defence, and so long as Britain was sovereign over Canada, it was her duty to defend Canada. If we were a colony still, we should have the right to claim this defence at the hands of the Mother Country. But to-day we are a free nation. Yet I have already said that we do owe a debt of gratitude to Great Britain. I proclaim it to the world. And why should we be grateful? Not because she has defended us, not because she has loaned us money, but because of the liberality of the regime she has introduced here. And especially do we of the province of Quebec owe gratitude to her-I say so without hesitation- because she has permitted us to become a nation within her Empire. That is the ground upon which I rest our gratitude to the Mother Country.
But, while I say this, I say also that if the basis of this contribution be gratitude, then the authors of this measure should blush. Who ever heard of paying gratitude with a loan? Favour begets favour. That being so, I could understand a gift as being an expression of gratitude. But this is not a gift that we are making to Great Britain; it is a loan. The Government on this question has been vacillating, changeable, variable, with an eye to the East and an eye to the West, trying one day to please the Imperialists and the next day to placate the Nationalists, and in the end deceiving all.
Sir, we are opposed to this contribution because our policy, as I said a moment ago, is a policy of autonomous development. That was the policy which was accepted in 1909 by both sides of this House; that was the policy which we endeavoured to put on the statute-book in 1910; and that is the policy to which we remain faithful. For remaining faithful to that policy we have brought down upon our heads the ire both of the Nationalists and of the Imperialists. Every day our policy is attacked in the Sir WILFRID LAURIER.
chief organ of Nationalism in the province of Quebec. Only last week there was published in that organ an article which opened with these sentences:
Mr. Laurier knows very well-and he proclaimed it in 1902 and 1907-that Canada, for the protection of its territory, and of its commerce, has no need of war vessels. Hei knows, and everybody knows, that England, the sole mistress and principal beneficiary of the maritime commerce of Canada, has a moral, legal and material obligation to defend that commerce; and he proclaimed himself against his opponents-in which he is right-that the British fleet is sufficiently powerful to accomplish that task. He knows also that if England were at war the trade of Canada would be carried under a neutral flag.
There are many things in this article which it is said I know, but which I know not, because they do not exist; there are other things which I do know, but which are not mentioned here. I know, for instance, and the writer of this article ought to know, that the British squadron has been removed from the northern waters of the Atlantic, the direct route of Canadian commerce. I know, moreover, that if Great Britain were at war Canadian trade would have to be carried under a neutral flag if there were no war vessels to protect it. That I know, and that is one reason for our policy. What would be the consequence if Canadian trade had to be carried under a neutral flag? It would mean that our exports-our cereals, butter, cheese, cattle, lumber, fish, minerals-in fact, all the products of the farm, the sea, the forest, the mine and the shop, would, if on the Atlantic coast, have to be taken to Boston and New York, and there placed in United States bottoms to be carried to their destination; or, if on the Pacific coast, would have to be carried to San Francisco, there to be placed in United States bottoms to be carried to their destination. This would mean that Canadian trade would be dislocated, that our harbours would be deserted, and that the people who usually handle this Canadian trade would be without their means of livelihood. These are the consequences which would follow if our trade were to be carried under a neutral flag, and it was to prevent that calamity that we decided to have a Canadian fleet of our own.
And what is the Imperialist side of our policy? We are every day taunted in this House and by the press throughout the country with the assertion that our naval service law of 1910, which created a Canadian navy, is a separatist law, and that our aims are towards separation. In connection with this I have a word to say to my hon. friend the Minister of Labour (Mr. Crothers). Some days ago the hon. minister delivered a speech in this House, in which he said, speaking of the election of Drummond and

Arthabaska, that, although I had for more than forty years been in the constituency, I had taken no part in that election, because my friends supporting the Liberal cause were preaching separation, and that if I had been there I would have had to bear, in the English provinces, the odium of the doctrine which was being preached in Drummond and Arthabaska. In order to do justice to the hon. the Minister of Labour, I will quote the very words he made use of. Speaking of the election, he said:
He did not appear amongst the people once during that campaign in Drummond and Arthabaska. Why? His followers carried forward that qampaign, and the burden of their song on every platform on which they spoke throughout the constituency was that the naval policy of the then leader of the Government meant separation, and had been adopted with a view to putting the people of Canada in a position to take care of themselves as soon as they became independent^ That was the doctrine preached from every platform in Drummond and Arthabaska during the first election held after the Naval Bill was introduced and carried in this House in 1910. Any hon. gentleman who desires to verify my remarks may do so by referring to the columns of the Montreal Herald and the .Montreal Witness, both Liberal papers, .where they will find, in the reports of the meetings held throughout Drummond and Arthabaska, that the Government of that day were preaching Canadian independence; and the right hon. leader of the Opposition, not desiring to incur in the English-speaking provinces the odium of supporting that doctrine, and not desiring to go into the constituency and say anything that would not be popular with the people, kept out of it altogether. What do hon. gentlemen think of a Prime Minister who, having introduced such a measure as the Naval Bill of 1910, and the first election after the passage of his Bill taking place in the constituency in which he lived for forty years, plays the coward, and keeps out of the constituency altogether.
Sir, there are big words in that paragraph. The word ' coward ' is a big one, even in the mouth of my hon. friend the Minister of Labour, who is not, he will admit, accustomed to remarkable feats of bravery. The hon. gentleman and I are good friends, I hope, but I am sure he will not take it amiss if I suggest that when he selects his adjectives, he had Better consult the record in order to ascertain whether or not they fit in with the subject. He gave very good advice to his hearers on that occasion when he suggested that they read the Montreal Witness and the Montreal Herald, both Liberal papers. If he had himself followed the advice he gave to others; if he had read the Montreal Witness, the Montreal Herald, the Montreal Gazette or the Montreal Star, he would never have spoken as he did, for he would have known that I was in Drummond and Arthabaska, and that I held the first meeting with my hon. friend the then Solicitor General, the member for Three Rivers (Mr. Bureau), when the candidature of Mr. Perreault, the Liberal candidate was being presented to the people. At that meeting, I spoke to perhaps one thousand electors, and set forth the policy of the Government of the day. I afiirm-and I challenge contradiction-that separation and disloyalty were preached, not by any member of the Liberal party, but by the men who are now supporting the Government and who sit in council with my hon friend the Minister of Labour (Mr. Crothers). Sir, it has been my privilege to speak upon that question both in the province of Ontario and the other English provinces and in the province of Quebec, and I defy my hon. friend or anybody else to find a word of contradiction between my speeches, whether I spoke in one province or the other.

How many times did the right hon. gentleman speak in Drummond and Arthabaska during the campaign, and at what time during the campaign did he make the speech to which he alludes? I remember very well-
Som hon. MEMBERS: Order.

Life is too
short for me at my age to undertake to reply to everything spoken of me. I do not remember the occasion to which my hon. friend refers. I may have been in the House or not; I do not know; but I know that the hon. gentleman had no right to make such a reference to me and to speak as he did. He wanted to convey the insinuation that I had raised racial cries I never did anything of the kind. On the contrary, everybody in Quebec knows that upon every platform from which I spoke- and there were scores of them-I told my fellow countrymen of French origin that it was their duty, if the supremacy of Great Britain were ever at stake, to risk their all in her defence. The statement of my hon. friend was unworthy of his position in this House. I know I have been taken to task again and again because I have asserted upon all these questions that parliament ought to have control of its policy. For this I have been branded in this House as a separatist.

But let us discuss this question, as I think we can, without any passion or prejudice. Sir, what is the meaning of the policy of the Government when they say they want to have a voice in all questions of peace and war, if it is not to affirm the supremacy of the Canadian Parliament? The Government want to have one of their ministers in London. What is that for? To discuss all questions of peace and war? What is that for? Is that minister in London to sit at the council board as a dummy? Is he to have no voice at all except to say ' yea ' to anything proposed, or is he to carry to London the views and the voice of the Canadian people? This is the policy which I have maintained all my life; this is the policy which I maintain to-day; and I believe that in his heart of hearts every man on the other side of the House will admit that there is no other policy to be maintained by a self-respecting people. The great mistake which is made by my Conservative friends on the other side of the House is that they will not trust the people, that they are afraid that if there should be an emergency, the Canadian people will not be up to the mark. We were put in that position in 1899 at the time of the South African war; but, Sir, without any compulsion, without any obligation on our part, when the flag was under trial in South Africa we determined that Canada should do her part, and we acted upon that determination. That is the true policy.
In the light of the discussion which has taken place, it has often occurred to me that we were approaching this subject from different points of view. It has seemed to me that the thought prevalent in the minds of hon. gentlemen opposite was that we are still a colony, whereas I maintain that we are now a nation. We are a nation within the British Empire; we are a nation consistently with our allegiance -to Great Britain; but it is one of the glories of Great Britain that she has allowed her colonies to develop into nationhood without forcing the breaking of the colonial ties. This is a development unique in history. It has brought about a condition in which the British Empire is composed of a galaxy of young, ardent nations. I do not know the view of our friends opposite-no, I think I know it; but, Sir, on this side of the House we take pride in claiming that we are a nation within the British Empire, and it is our policy to take up the duties which pertain to nationhood. This is one of the reasons why I oppose this policy. We oppose this policy because it does not recognize the duty which we owe to ourselves as a nation. We oppose this policy because it is not based on principle, but is simply makeshift and expedient. We oppose this policy because, as stated by one of the leaders of hon.
Sir WILFRID LAURIER.
gentlemen opposite, it does not strike any root, it does not prepare the soil, it leaves no residue. We oppose this policy because this $35,000,000 should be applied to the organization of a Canadian naval service in close co-operation with and in connection with the Imperial navy- a Canadian service, built, manned, equipped, in Canada. This is the goal to which we are looking; and it is because the present policy ignores all these duties that we say, revert to the old policy which we all accepted in 1909 and which should be accepted in 1913, and which we in opposition as in office maintained flying to the winds. It is for these reasons that we say we cannot support this policy. My last word is that we cannot support it, and I beg to move the six months' hoist.

I was myself, Mr. Speaker, on the point of submitting the motion which has just been made by the hon. leader of the Opposition, but not however for the same reasons.
The hon. leader of the Opposition is asking for the six-months' hoist. Why so? Simply, so as to be able to come back to his own naval law. That law has already been condemned by the people. For my part, I have condemned it myself, and I have done all I could to have it condemned by others. The Liberal party is now opposed to a temporary policy, so as to give new life to a permanent policy. Do you call that sincerity?
Amendments upon amendments have been proposed, the better apparently to destroy a law which is approved in principle. Both parties seem to have come to the same understanding upon the fact that it is necessary that money should be spent for the motherland. But the hon. leader of the Opposition goes still farther, when he says that money does not suffice for paying a debt of gratitude, and that he is ready to contribute, even by calling upon our children to shed their blood, in reverting to the Naval Policy which he has formerly patronized and which he desires to revive to-day. For my part, I am opposed to that policy, and if I have condemned in the past the policy of the leader of the Opposition, I must also condemn to-day the policy of the Government. Those two policies, I condemn absolutely, and I feel certain that the country also condemns them.
A short time ago, I had the honour to ask the leader of the Government to refer that measure of contribution to the people, by way of a referendum, and also refer in the same time the measure of the preceding administration. I say again, I believe that is the only way to know clearly and without ambiguity how public opinion stands on that matter. But both parties have come to an understanding that such an

amendment, as I had the honour to propose, must be killed.
It is a conspiracy.

Yes, there is a conspiration, but that conspiration is one of both parties to spend the money of a people who refuses to spend anything for armaments; it is a conspiration of both parties to stifle the voice of the people.
That is the hobby of Bourassa.

It gives me pleasure to support the motion of the hon. leader of the Opposition, but, I say again, not for the reasons that he has given himself.
When it was said that the independent members were not loyal, that was an error, and the people has been deceived when there were attributed to independent papers certain articles and carieatures which those papers have never published, but which were, as stated this morning by the hon. Prime Minister, a pure invention of the Liberals and of the 'Canada.' The same tactics will be continued, in telling deliberate falsehood. They will say, in Ontario, that the Independents are not loyal enough, and, in Quebec, that such a contribution will ruin the country. It is a reversion to the same game.
With regard to a permanent policy, the hon. Prime Minister has declared that he would never commit himself to such a policy without first consulting the people. But, for my part, I must object energetically against taking the first steps in that direction, in voting to-day a contribution, even if only temporary. It is for that reason that I will vote in favour of the amendment of the -leader of the Opposition, but not for the motives he has stated.
I desire to say a few words in English to make my position clear to those who do not understand French. I am in favour of this amendment, and am prepared to second it, but not for the reasons given by the right hon. the leader of the Opposition. The leader of the Opposition has in view the keeping in force of the Canadian Naval Service Act, but I stated in the province of Quebec, and everywhere I spoke, that I was opposed to that Act, and my friends and I are equally opposed to this'Bill, though, I repeat, not for the same reasons as the leader of the Opposition.

There
are many others like you.
You are not.

No, I am not, thank
God.

The people are, and I am with the people. I simply wish to repeat that I second the motion of the leader of the Opposition, but for reasons
quite opposed to those given by my right hon. friend.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. L. BORDEN (Prime Minister) :
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, there seems to have been some competition between my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition, and the hon. member for Joliette for the honour of moving the six months' hoist in respect of this Bill. My hon. friend from Joliette (Mr. Guilbault) rose before six o'clock, but gave way when the Speaker called upon the right hon. the leader of the Opposition, and thus the right hon. gentleman secured the first opportunity in that regard. I will not follow the right hon. gentleman in all his observations. He has alluded to the ruthless closure which took place after the second clause of this Bill had been discussed in committee for twenty days. If that is ruthless closure, then my right hon. friend is under some hardship in respect to the matter. But I have been reminded by one hon. gentleman on the other side of the House that I need have no apprehension that they have not had ample opportunity to discuss this Bill to their heart's content. The right hon. gentleman still harps upon the question of an appeal to the people. When, in 1910, he put forward what he expressly stated to be a definite and permanent policy for the people of this country, he voted on at least two occasions, and I think on three occasions that there should be no appeal to the people before the permanent policy was adopted. When, in tne light of the Admiralty memorandum which has been placed before this House, we now propose that there should be this temporary measure of immediate and effective aid, my right hon. friend departs from the position which he took in 1910, and demands that there should be an appeal to the people before any further steps are taken. He does that, notwithstanding that he himself, and all his followers voted on 13th February, and again on 27th February, that there should be a grant of $35,000,000, although it was to be spent in a different way.
That is not new.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
My hon. friend has
spoken a good many times on this question, without, I think, contributing anything new to the debate. Now the right hon. gentleman has discovered what he considers absolute and conclusive evidence that there is no emergency, and no need, and that Canada should stay her hand and do nothing at this moment. He bases that upon his allegation that these ships are not, as he says, to be in the firing line at all, because they are to be placed, not in the North sea, but at Gibraltar. Has my right hon. friend so neglected to observe what has taken place in the British House of Commons during



the past year that he does not know the object of placing the Mediterranean fleet at Gibraltar instead of at Malta? It was stated in very plain terms indeed by the First Lord of the Admiralty less than a year ago, and the ground which the First Lord of the Admiralty put forward at that time was that these ships were within two or three steaming days of the North sea and could be called upon in case of emergency to join their forces with those which were already there for the defence of the whole Empire. My right hon. friend suggests that this fleet is to be under the guns of Gibraltar and that it is not to do any fighting at all. Let me distinguish between this fleet and that which my right hon. friend proposed in 1910. This is a fighting fleet of five of the most formidable battle cruisers in the world which can go to the North sea, or to the Mediterranean, or to the North Atlantic, or to Australia, or to the Pacific, or wherever the needs of defence may call it. It is not a fleet that is not designed for fighting. On the contrary, it will be a fleet possessing the greatest speed of any fleet in the world of a similar character, a fleet composed of armoured cruisers of the most powerful and modern type and one which will be able to afford every needed aid which the requirements of the Empire may demand.
But my right hon. friend harps upon the question of the Canadian Naval Service which he instituted in 1910. He asserts, in so far as I understand his argument, that we should stay our hand until we aTe able to build that fleet completely in Canada. If my right hon. friend did not mean that by his previous speeches it will be well for him to say so now. As I understand his proposals, no part of the money ought to be expended outside of Canada and in face of the conditions disclosed in the Admiralty memorandum, we should stay our hand in Canada, as he stayed his hand for fifteen years when in power, and await the day when we shall have the ability in this country to construct not only the hulls of these battleships but the armour-plate, the armament, the guns and all of the countless variety of engines and machinery that are necessary for the thorough equipment of a dreadnought. What does that mean? Every hon. gentleman in this House knows the indefinite delay which that means. Every one remembers the delay which my right hon. friend insisted upon, in 1902 and again in 1907 at the Imperial conferences. I have his language under my hand and I could quote it to the House if I were disposed to do so, but I make the assertion in the bald terms which I have used and I challenge my right hon. friend to a Mr. BOLDEN.
contradiction of what I have stated. He will not contradict it because he knows that I speak by the record.
He ventured to assert that in 1909 a certain resolution was passed by this House and that he undertook to carry out that resolution by his proposal of 1910. I venture to affirm that he did not undertake to carry out, by the Naval Service Act of 1910, the resolution which was agreed to in this House in 1909. The resolution of this House in 1909 declared for a naval service in Canada to be in close corporation with the naval service of the Empire and along the lines suggested at the last Imperial conference. The lines suggested at the last Imperial conference were that in time of war all the naval forces of the Empire should be united to repel any attack, that they should be under one direction and control, and that they should not be organized as scattered navies which might be overcome in succession by a hostile power.
But the emergency has ceased, repeats my right hon. friend, although he did mot lay emphasis upon it. He said that there is no emergency, that there is no need, and his followers have stated time and again that Great Britain is wealthy, that Great Britain is disposed to maintain her naval forces so that the Empire cannot be successfully attacked and, therefore, why should we take any steps ? There is no emergency, said my right hon. friend, there is no need, there is no occasion for us to take any step whatever. But I would like to point out to him that one of his own colleagues, and a very leading colleague, I believe, the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver), a little more than a year ago in this House, said this:
If there was necessity to prepare for naval defence two years ago, how much greater is that necessity to-day? Two years ago there was merely a suspicion of danger, but today Germany and England are exchanging what are practically defiances. It is admitted that the only security which the British Empire has to-day is the British fleet; and that without that fleet the prestige of Britain would be gone and the liberties of Canada^ would be endangered.
Further on:
I say that the Empire admittedly, never since the days of Napoleon the First, has been in greater danger than it has been within the past two months. Does anybody deny it?
And again:
But I say that under the circumstances which have occurred during the past two months, when only yesterday the telegraph wires were awaiting and expecting war, these gentlemen cannot escape responsibility by saying that they have no policy.

I have quotation after quotation from the leading Liberal organ of hon. gentlemen opposite published in Ontario in which, during the past summer, the same statement is made. These views were put forward only some eight or nine months ago. which goes with the citation that I have just read from the language of Sir Edward Grey on the 7th day of April last.
Let me say just one or two words with regard to the Naval Service Act of 1910. It is well we should have a clear understanding on this question. I do not propose to make any personal attack upon my right hon. friend in respect of any opinions which he now holds or which he may hereafter hold with regard to the co-operation of this country in the naval defence of the Empire. The right hon. gentleman is thoroughly entitled to his opinions, and other hon. gentlemen in this House and in this country are entitled also to their opinions; but I call his attention to the fact that from 1902 to 1911, so far as I understand his attitude, it was that of one who was determined that Canada should not take any real part in the naval defence of the Empire. I have under my hand a statement made recently by Mr. Merriman in a debate in the Parliament of South Africa. Mr. Merriman's statement as to the attitude which the right hon. gentleman took in that conference, in which he was a colleague of my right hon. friend on many occasions, is-
He was at none of the conferences which I attended.
