My right hon. friend has held his opinions on that subject in days gone by. He alluded to them in his speech on the 12th of December last, when he spoke of his utterances as being those of his boyhood days. I would like to remind my right hon. friend, and I do so in the kindest possible manner, that the utterances to which allusion was made were not utterances of his boyhood days; they Mr. BORDEN.
were utterances after he had been twenty years in this Parliament, and after he had been five years leader of his paTty. That perhaps is a significant circumstance which ought not to be overlooked by the right hon. gentleman when he deals with that particular matter.
Let us come now to the Canadian Naval Service Act of 1910. Hon. gentlemen opposite have stated over and over again in this debate that this Bill on it3 face seemed more or less harmless; but that it was to be interpreted in the light of my speech in introducing it, and in the light of my subsequent remarks in regard to it. I am quite ready to assent to that suggestion in so far as the Bill and the speech which accompanied it are indicative of the policy of the party which I have the honour to lead. If that be the true principle with regard to this Bill, and my utterances in respect of it, I assume that it is equally a true and proper principle to apply to the Naval Service Act of 1910, as interpreted by the speeches of my right hon. friend in support of it. The right hon. gentleman has a certain conception of Canada's duty towards the Empire, and I have another, which seem to be entirely distinct and divergent. The conception of the right hon. gentleman, if I understand it, i3 that Canada should have a naval service of its own; that the ships belonging to that naval service may be neutral in time of war and will be so, unless the Governor in Council passes an order that they shall take part; that even our shores and harbours may be neutral in time of war; that is to say, the right hon. gentleman's conception is a Canadian naval service absolutely distinct and separate from the naval service of the Mother Country and the rest of the Empire; that we should have no voice or influence in the councils of the Empire which determine war or peace, and that we may possibly be neutral in time of war. According to his conception, we are to enjoy the advantages which result from belonging to this Empire in time of peace, and then when war comes we are to judge as to the justice of the quarrel, and if we do not think the quarrel just we are to pass no Order in Council, we do not call Parliament together-because in case of inaction according to the Act of 1910 Parliament is not called together-and Canada's ships, and I suppose, Canada's shores and harbours are to remain neutral. I d.o not think my hon. friend opposite is misrepresented by what I have just stated. If he thinks he is, I will read to him his own words so that there may be no possible doubt on the subject. I quote from the debate on this subject which took place in this House in 1910:

Mr. Borden: Would the right hon. gentleman permit me to ask him a question? Suppose a Canadian ship meets a ship of similar armament and power belonging to an enemy, meets her on the high seas, what is she to do? I do not ask now what she will do, if attacked; but will she attack, will she fight?
Sir Wilfrid Laurier:	I do not know that
she would fight. I do not know that she should fight either. She should not fight until the Government by which she is commissioned have determined whether she should go into the war. That is the position we take; my hon. friend takes a different position. He says that without any question, under all circumstances, we are bound to send our ships into the war. We take a different position, and we say: Let the country judge between us.

what my hon. friend means by asking if they should be neutral.
Mr. Borden. I understand the Prime Minister to say that our ships would not fight until they were ordered to do so, and, therefore, they would in effect be neutral untill the Governor in Council had made an order; that they should participate in the war. Have I misstated my hon. friend's position?

When my hon. friend is frank enough to give me an answer, I may go on and discuss that subject. Now, every hon. member of this House is entitled to his opinion, and I have explained the position of hon. gentlemen as I understand it. I have shown how their Canadian Naval Service will be neutral in time of war unless an Order in Council is passed, and they contend that the Canadian Naval Service shall not necessarily take part in Britain's wars. We have several illustrations given by my right hon. friend. I have these also under my hand. We have him reported as stating that if
the Crimean War were to be fought over again and we had a Canadian Naval Service, if he were Prime Minister those Canadian ships would be neutral and would take no part in the war. We have him further stating that if the demonstration against Egypt at Alexandria were to take place again and Canada had a Naval Service, and he were Prime Minister, that Naval Service would be neutral and would take no part in the war-and as a result, I assume, would take no part in any war growing out of that demonstration. The British navy has been the protection of Canada, of Canadian ships, of Canadian commerce, of Canadians throughout the world. We have had no other protection so far as the high seas are concerned. Suppose this country became embroiled through some act of its own with another power; suppose we enforced some law harshlv: and suppose our enforcement of that law did not commend itself to the judgment of the Government	of the United Kingdom
is the rule to work both ways?- is Great Britain to say:	Our navy
shall not protect you Canadians, your coasts or your shipping, until we pass an Order in Council; and as we do not think yo-ur quarrel just we will pass no Order in Council and you can fight this battle unaided and alone? Does any hon. member of this House believe this Empire of ours could be kept together by anv nolicv such as that?	*
What is the other conception as to our duty in this respect? The other contention is this: that we may have a Canadian division or unit of the British navy, if you like, because a just pride and sentiment of the Canadian people may desire to recognize in the British army a particular division which shall be distinctively Canadian, but that all the forces of the Empire shall be united in time of war and shall stand together to repel any invader or assailant whether the attack is directed against the British Islands, or Canada, or any other dominion of the Empire. And, concurrently with that, I have taken the ground, and I think it is a just ground, that when we reach the position of assuming a definite and established part in the naval defence of the Empire, then, inasmuch as the question of defence is connected with the question of foreign policy, with the councils of the Empire which determine peace or war, then we, as Canadians, desire to have a just voice in those councils. Hon. gentlemen on the other side seem to be alarmed by such a proposal; they say it is a recession, a denial of our autonomy. I venture to submit to the judgment of every hon. gentleman of thi9 House that it is not a recession but a continuance of that constitutional

development which we have had in this country for the last seventy-five years. What did we accomplish first after the troubles of 1837? We got responsible government, responsibility of the executive to the people, the absolute control of Parliament over the revenues of the country. Then, we got control of our public lands; they were thereafter managed not in the Mother Country, but by the Canadian Parliament and the Canadian executive. Then, we got absolute control of our fiscal policy. Then, we advanced to the dignity of making our own commercial treaties. So, from the rudiments of self-government which prevailed before 1837, we have by degrees advanced to a period when Canada is a nation within the Empire, having practically complete power of self-government. And is it not a legitimate development of that increase in power and influence, that we should also claim some voice in the councils of the Empire which determine peace and war, especially as, according to my conception, Canada, if she remains within the Empire,_ i?rust be involved in any war in which the Empire is involved. This theory of neutrality which appeals to hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House does not seem capable of standing any close or searching analysis. I observe in the press despatches this morning that the Rev. Dr. J. T. Lawrence, formerly deputy professeor of international law in the University of Cambridge, has been discussing the relations of the dominions with the Mother Country in this connection, and, in stating his conclusions, the report says:
In connection with the question of neutrality, he laid it down that^ the great self-governing colonies could not invoke the principle of limited liability in war. All parts of the Empire must sink or swim together.
Further on he says:
Hence arose the disposition to claim that their armed forces should be entirely under their own control, and he did not think that Great Britain disputed that. But neutrality and belligerency were the functions of the sovereigns states. A power could be no more neutral in one port and belligerent in another than a man could be married in one. part and single in another part of the country.
No foreign country would recognize any such in-and-out arrangements, if ever an attempt was seriously made to create a curious race of international entities. We should be British at one moment and non-British at the next, an in-and-out policy which would 6urely break down.
So I say that if you take the two conceptions and place them side by side and contrast them, any hon. gentleman in this House who sincerely desires that Canada shall work out her destiny within the Em-Mr. BORDEN.
pire will surely come to the conclusion not that we shall have separate navies, neutral if you like, in time of war; not that we shall have no voice or influence in the councils of the Empire, but that we shall have, if you like, a distinctively Canadian portion of the Imperial navy, that that distinctively Canadian portion of that navy shall be part of the armed forces of the Empire in time of war, and that we as Canadians shall have our voice and influence in the councils of the Empire which determine peace or war. This seems to me a more reasonable and logical conclusion as to our future relations with the Mother Country than that which my right hon. friend on the other side of the House proposes. No one appreciates more than I do the difficulty of the problems that will arise in working out any permanent scheme of co-operation in this respect between the great dominions and the Mother Country. I have said before that the problem is attendant with great difficulties, but the mere fact that it is attendant with great difficulties surely ought not to deter the statesmen of the Mother Country or of the great dominions of the Empire from giving their best consideration to an endeavour at least to take the same step in advance. In the proposition which I outlined on December 5 last, I indicated a certain important step which we may take at this time. That step has been criticised, but I know it is regarded by statesmen of the Mother Country on both sides of the Imperial House as a step not only proper and desirable, but as one which in the future may lead to a very important advance, and which, while preserving the autonomy of the great dominions of the Empire, will give to them a reasonable voice and influence in the councils of the Empire that determine peace or war.
There are a great many things that Canada can do to aid the Mother Country aside from the provision of these ships. Canada can take very important steps in regard to matters that are entirely under her own control, and as to which there can be no possible suggestiqn that her autonomy will be disturbed in any way. Take, for example, the construction of dry-docks, which, while perhaps primarily useful for commercial purposes, could be constructed under Admiralty supervision and would be an important aid to the Admiralty in time of war. It is the intention of the Government to proceed with the construction of dry-docks on the Atlantic and Pacific coasts. The question of a dry-dock in the St. Lawrence at Quebec has been under discussion in this House, and inasmuch as there are, I think, some twenty or twenty-two steamships in the St. Lawrence which cannot be accommo-

dated by any dock	below Montreal
at the present time, I venture to say	that every	hon.	gentleman
in this House will be glad to approve of the action of the Government in that regard. At Halifax and on the Pacific coast the docking facilities are also inadequate, and it is the purpose of the Government to at once to proceed with the construction of dry-docks at these points as well, the construction of each one being an important aid not only to the shipping and commerce of this country but to the Admiralty as well, if, unfortunately, war should break out and their ships should require the services of one of these docks for purposes of repair. We can take another important step by establishing naval bases on the Atlantic and Pacific entirely within our own control, and we can undertake the fortification of trie harbours and ports at which these naval bases may be constructed. Not only can we undertake the fortification of these ports by batteries on shore, but we can provide for their defence as well by torpedo boats and other similar craft, in regard to which we would seek the advice and assistance of the Admiralty. I have already stated in this House that it is not desirable that all the ship-building facilities of the Empire should be concentrated in the United Kingdom. That has been assented to by the Lords of the Admiralty, for they have commended the establishment and gradual extension in the overseas dominions of ship-building and repair plants, capable in the first place of building small cruisers and other ancillary craft, as well as vessels for commercial purposes. These eventually might be so extended-and would, we hope, be so extended-that they would be capable of constructing vessels of a very much larger size. We believe it is in the public interest that we should encourage this establishment and extension, and I stated on the 5th of December last that the Admiralty proposed to co-operate with us in that purpose by giving orders for small cruisers and other auxiliary craft to be built in this country provided we can assure them that those craft can be built in such manner and within such time as to compare reasonably with the construction of similar vessels in the United Kingdom. Then we can proceed with the training of officers in the naval college at Halifax and by means of training-ships maintained for that purpose; and it would be well, I think, that the ships of the Canadian hydrographic survey and of the Canadian fisheries protection service should be manned by men so trained. Mr. Churchill, in speaking on this subject on March 26 last, used this language:
Side by side with this the dominions will
be encouraged by the Admiralty to develop the necessary naval bases, dockyards, cruisers, local flottillas, or other ancillary craft, which
will enable the Imperial squadron to operate for a prolonged period m any particular threatened theatre to which it might be sent.
We have a fisheries protection service in this country, and that service might be amplified and developed to a much greater extent than it has been in the past by the addition of small cruisers, which while primarily used for the purpose of protecting our fisheries and natural resources against marauders, would, in time of war, be useful for the protection of our commerce and for the purpose alluded to by Mr. Churchill in the citation I have just read. It will be observed, therefore, that in all this there is room for the Canadian people to undertake very much that will be absolutely important for the protection of our own harbours and coasts and commerce within a certain area, and at the same time will be of a character to afford material assistance to the proposals of the Admiralty as outlined by Mr. Churchill.
I venture to think that when the hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House propose, as they have proposed, that we should establish two fleet units in this country and man them altogether in Canada, they are absolutely oblivious of the consideration which I have brought to their attention some weeks ago when I pointed out that the training of seamen and of artificers and machinists for the royal navy is a work which occupies a very considerable number of years. Create two fleet units in Canada and man them by Canadians at once ? Why the figures I gave to this House on a former occasion indicate the absolute impossibility of doing that. What are the conditions in regard to the Niobe and the Rainbow to which hon. gentlemen opposite have very frequently alluded ? The conditions are that much the larger proportion of the men in training on these ships are not Canadians. I have said before that this is no discredit to Canadians, because the numerous opportunities in the ordinary avocations of life in this country do not tend to induce Canadians to enter the naval service. My right hon. friend knows his own experience in connection with the Royal Northwest Mounted Police. I took that force over as he left it, and what is its position? Not more than seventeen per cent of the men in the Royal Northwest Mounted Police to-day are native-born Canadians, seventy or seventy-five per cent were bom in the British Isles and about eleven per cent were not born within the British dominions at all. What is the position so far as the permanent military force of Canada is concerned? Something like eighty per cent of the members of the permanent force were born in the British Isles. This is no discredit to Canadians, because

of the abundant opportunities on every side in this country for men in other walks of life. Not only the Royal Northwest Mounted Police and the permanent force, but the Canadian naval service are manned very largely by men who have come from the British Isles.
Hon. gentlemen opposite have taken the ground that this Government has no mandate whatever for making these proposals to Parliament. They say, in effect, that we did not place any such policy before the people of Canada, that the people have never pronounced upon it, and that therefore there should be an appeal to the people. In 1910 I made the distinct proposal in this House that a sufficient sum to provide two battleships or armoured cruisers of the most modern and powerful type should be provided for the needs of the naval forces of the Empire at that time. In November, 1910, I declared in this Parliament that if we were returned to power at the next election we would proceed to ascertain from the Admiralty what the needs of the Empire were, and if we were convinced that the needs of the Empire demanded immediate and effective assistance from Canada, we would ask Parliament for that immediate and effective assistance. And in the campaign of 1911, speaking at London in the province of Ontario, in the very first speech that I made in that campaign, I declared the same thing to the people of Ontario and of all Canada, and I have the quotation here under my hand. My right hon. friend himself, speaking at Soxel in the province of Quebec, during the campaign of 1911. used this language on the 23rd day of August:
Mr. Borden's idea is to vote $25,000,000 and give it to England. Do you want a navy actually made and manned in Canada or do you want to make an annual contribution
to England ?
My right hon. friend was not accurately representing my policy as I had presented it before Parliament but he did indicate to the people of Canada that I had made proposals of a distinct and definite character, and thus he made it abundantly clear to those whom he addressed and to the people of Canada to whom his language was repeated through the press that there were two distinct policies before the people of Canada at that time, and that my policy was to bring immmediate and effective aid to the Empire by the methods which I now ask Parliament to sanction.
Under these circumstances, having regard to what I said in 1910 in February and again in November of the same year, having regard to the speech wiith which I opened the campaign in the province of Ontario in that year, having regard to what the leader of the Opposition himself Mr. BORDEN.
presented before the electorate in the province of Quebec as a contrast between the policies on the one hand and on the other, I fail to apprehend the argument of hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House when they declare that the Government has no mandate to propose this policy or to ask Parliament to sanction it. Why, Mr. Speaker, this Parliament and this Government have a more direct mandate to pass this law' than my right hon. friend's Government and the then Parliament which he led ever had to pass any of the important measures which he put through this Parliament during his whole fifteen years in office. If any hon. gentleman on the other side of the House will point to any important measure that they ever put through this Parliament in respect of which they had as direct a mandate from the people of Canada as that which we hold in regard to this important question, there might be some force in the argument which they adduced. These proposals of ours will afford immediate aid to the naval forces of the Empire from a material standpoint. But there is the other standpoints to which my hon. friend alluded, the moral support and strength which they bring to the Empire. It is to be regretted that a few hon. gentleman on the other side of the House have seen fit to speak with some exultation of their efforts in destroying that moral support and influence which otherwise would be drawn from this measure. This is not, it seems to me, the spirit which should animate men who are earnestly and patriotically desirous of doing something which we regard as necessary and urgent in the interests of the whole Empire, because this proposal is not for Great Britain alone, it is not for Canada alone; our proposal is to build three battleships of the most modern and powerful type and to place them at the disposal of His Majesty the King for the common defence of the whole Empire. That is our policy. If hereafter, the people of Canada should decide upon the policy of establishing a fleet unit on the Atlantic and another on the Pacific; the ships we propose	to construct
could be utilized for that purpose. They might in all probability be so utilized even before they were put in commission. It is most unfortunate that this view has not impressed itself upon hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House. So far as we are concerned, we believe that when half of the forces of the Empire which uphold the flag in all the oceans, and upon all the seas, have been withdrawn to protect the heart of the Empire, when even the Mediterranean itself has been left very largely unguarded, the time has come when in a spirit of self-respect, Canada should assert

her place in the Empire, and should proclaim to the world the unity of that Empire for purposes of defence. The time has come when our friends opposite should no longer quibble about this proposal, but should join with us in bringing immediate and effective aid, as we propose by the measure which we have placed before the House.
Hon. GEO. P. GRAHAM (South Renfrew): The question that we are discussing tonight is one in which the parties have been divided since 1909, but on which they were unanimous at that time. In taking the view I do with hon. gentlemen behind and beside me, we do not admit for one moment that we are less loyal than the men on the Government benches. We may not talk so much about it. We may not present each other with Union Jacks every time we have a meeting; the actions of the Liberal party speak louder than the words of my hon. friends opposite. My right hon. friend a moment ago spoke of the dilatoriness of the Liberal Government for many years in not doing something for the British Empire in the matter of naval defence. He forgot that Canada has been growing and developing along lines of nationhood, and that years ago she was not in a position 'to do what she is able to do to-day. Every reader of history knows that. But speaking of dilatoriness in regard to the British Empire, the friends of my right hon. friend were in the ascendancy in this House for 18 years, and with all their professions of loyalty they never gave the Mother Land a preference for her goods in the Canadian market, and it remained for the Liberals to do so.
They opposed it.

I might go further and say they opposed it, and I presume they would oppose it now. My right hon. friend discussed pretty freely the powers of war and the duty of men to be warlike. Canada, he said, should take her place in the firing line, whenever that may be. It is a movable feast now apparently. While he was speaking my mind was attracted to the other side of the question, and I desire to ask the members of this House whether it is not worth while to halt a moment, and whether, as a young country, in co-operation with the great British Empire, we should not dwell a little more on the blessings of peace in this country, rather than dilate on the triumphs of war. At the present moment we are joining with the other parts of the British Empire, and with the United States, in preparing for a celebration of peace, and Sir, while we have to maintain our equipment as a nation, we ought to hesitate before we go beyond the line of that equipment, and talk of putting ships in the line of aggressiveness, to provoke war, according to some hon. gentlemen rather than to prevent it. Lord Morley, in the ripeness of his years, is going to Germany, and, I think, will be an important factor in the discussion of the question not of building more great battleships, but of decreasing them. I think we ought to hesitate before we lay all the stress of, all the strength of our argument on the necessity of preparing for war. After all, in a coun. try like this, where, for 100 years we have lived side by side with another great country without any sign of disturbance, without the need of a gun pointing either way, for aggression or for defence, we ought to lay the lessons of peace to heart more than the lessons of war. In the years to come, no matter how much we may prepare, no matter how much attention we may pay to the defences of the country, I predict that the monuments in Canada will be to the triumphs of peace, and not to the aggressiveness and bloodshed of war.
My right hon. friend's remarks were under two or three heads. One was the emergency. That emergency is very elusive. It has been gathered to its fathers, and it has departed unwept, unhonoured, and unsung. Notwithstanding the attempts of my right hon. friend to work up enthusiasm over it, he could not place his finger anywhere in the British Empire where there is an emergency at the present time. It started in the North sea, and the First Lord of the Admiralty has moved_ it to Gibraltar, and attached it to a flying squadron, and I really do not know where it will arise next as the Prime Minister tonight chased it to Bulgaria. We might as well admit and hon. gentlemen in this House and the people of the country know it, that there is no emergency. I admit there is a need. What is the need? For a temporizing policy? I desire to point out that we as a young nation, in our strength, development and increasing manhood, should not continue to ask the Mother Country to do for us what we are clearly able to do for ourselves. Let us undertake to do the work that falls to us as a part of the British Empire; let us take a course which will demonstrate to the world that we are an integral portion of the Empire. Let us do our duty like men, not only by engaging in the construction of ships, but in the protection of our own shores, our -own commerce and our own trade routes. Let us be ready when duty calls to fight side by side with the Motherland not with empty ships, but with ships manned by Canadians, built, so far as possible, in Canada, and maintained by Canadian taxpayers.

Before the Bill passes into the unknown future, I feel it my duty to say a few words with regard to this very important matter.

This discussion, which has recurred at intervals during a period of several months, has been engaged in on the assumption that war is a necessity, and that active preparation for war is a means of preventing it. Wars have always engaged the active attention of mankind, and yet men have always believed that some day wars would cease. I am of the belief that that day has now come, and in the few remarks I propose to make will keep that consideration in view. We have heard during the course of this de-oate of the wonderful development in the art of building armoured battle ships. Eighteen nations are actively engaged in building battleships, and fourteen of these nations commenced their construction within the last twenty years. The tendency is to build larger ships all the time and to increase the number. In England there are battleships of 25,000 tons; in Japan, where they never built one of these ships until 1897, they are now building three of 27,500 tons and in some of the South American republics they have still larger ships of 28,000 tons In the United States they never built a battleship until 1893, in 1897 they had only six but since that they have built eighty-three. All the civilized nations are straining every nerve to increase the number of battleships they possess. Immense armies and navies are kept in readiness to fight and defend, the whole world a battlefield, war inscribed on every banner and peace forgotten, Canada alone standing out so far, like a bright star in a dark sky, but liable to fall at any moment. These are impressions that one must get in listening to the discussion which has been going on. I said that fourteen of these nations only commenced building battleships in the last twenty years. I find in that time the nations have spent for army and navy purposes the immense sum of thirty-one thousand millions of dollars; just think of it, thirty-one thousand millions of dollars wasted within the last twenty years, and the annual expenditure to-day is twenty-five hundred million dollars, That total warlike expenditure among the nations ranges from 10 per cent in some nations to nearly 50 per cent in otheT nations of the total expenditure for all purposes of these nations. What is the cause of this? Why is it that there is this mad feeling of waste in all the nations? Why is it that before any naval appropriation is made in any legislative assembly in the world it is preceded by a war scare? It is because the people listen to the voice of the inhuman gods of war and of the navy leagues the world over, who are willing to traffic in the blood of their fellow men for gain. They play one nation against another. When a battleship is built it is a notice to other nations to build. We build, you build and so the mad waste goes on. Does anyone suppose that armaments are Mr. CHARI/TON.
an insurance premium of peace? They are more justly called a menace to peace. That this congress emphatically recommends to all nations the establishment of a permanent international court of arbitral justice, of free and easy access, composed of judges representing the various juridical systems of the world and capable of ensuring continuity in jurisprudence of arbitration.
